Special Scales

Symmetry, color, and pull.

The diminished and whole-tone systems, the bebop scales, and the hexatonic colors — the tools that don't fit modal furniture.

Half–Whole Diminished

1 · ♭2 · ♭3 · 3 · ♯4 · 5 · 6 · ♭7

The native scale of dom7♭9, ♯9, ♯11, 13. Any V7 heading to a I∆.

  • Symmetric — only three transpositions exist
  • Any dom7♭9 = diminished 7 with root on the 3rd (G7♭9 → B°7) (NK 2021-12-17 · 11:01–11:50)

Whole–Half Diminished

1 · 2 · ♭3 · 4 · ♭5 · ♭6 · 6 · 7

Over °7 chords directly.

  • Sub the vi in a iii–vi with ♭iii°7 (Em–A7 → Em–E♭°7)
  • Sub for dom7♭9 up a half step (G7♭9 → A♭°7)

Whole Tone

1 · 2 · 3 · ♯4 · ♯5 · ♭7

Only two whole-tone scales exist. Pure suspension.

  • Over dom7♯11♭13 resolving to I∆7
  • Sit on it — let it drift. Resolves itself.

Hexatonic Major

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · ♭6

First six tones of harmonic major. Santangelo's secret door.

  • A♭7♯11 · G7alt · Cm∆7 with B♭ · E♭ · G hex — see James Santangelo
  • Implies: I+, ii7♭5, IIIalt, iv∆, V7♭9, VImaj7♭13, ♭VII7♯11, vii°7

Hexatonic Altered

1 · ♭2 · ♭3 · 3 · ♭6 · ♭7

Altered without the ♭5. The "V7alt hex" of choice. (OS clip maness hexatonic scale · 00:00–00:43)

  • G7alt hex omits D♭
  • Pairs with altered pentatonic for layered tension

Bebop Dominant

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · 6 · ♭7 · 7

Eight-note scale tuned so chord tones land on downbeats. Over any dom7.

  • Bebop Maj6: 1 2 3 4 5 ♯5 6 7 — over ∆7
  • Bebop m6: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♯5 6 7 — over m6 / m∆7
Pentatonics

Five notes, endless rooms.

The vocabulary that pours through every great solo — and the rules for where each one lives.

Major Pentatonic

1 · 2 · 3 · 5 · 6

The default major-key voice. Bright, open, unfussy.

  • I∆7, ii7, vi7, VI∆7
  • ♭VII7♯11 (lydian dominant)
  • Voiced as a five-note set and its four rotations — one set for B♭6/9, G–7, E♭∆7, C7sus and A♭∆7♯11: see the Magic Voicing System in Comping
  • Pentatonic triads skip a note twice — F A D, G C F, A D G, C F A, D G C up F major pentatonic — over F, Dm7, B♭∆7, G7sus and E♭∆7♯11; dyads skip one note, down E minor pentatonic with a turn, over Em – C∆ – A7sus – F∆. (OS clip maness pentatonic chords · 00:00–00:46; OS clip maness warmup pentatonic dyad · 00:00–00:44)
  • On ♭5 of dom7alt — G♭ major pentatonic over C7alt; over E♭7 the same move gives A major pentatonic, the tritone sub’s own — A B C♯ E F♯ = ♯11 ♭13 ♭7 ♭9 ♯9. E minor pentatonic (E G A B D) is a different set. (this page's reading)

Minor Pentatonic

1 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 · ♭7

The workhorse. Every chord type has one waiting for it.

  • Over dom7: minor pentatonic up a whole step (Am over G7)
  • Over m7: on the 1, 2, and 5 (Dm, Em, Am over Dm7)
  • Over ∆7: down a 3rd, plus 5th, plus 5th-above

Dorian Pentatonic

1 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 · 6

Minor pentatonic with the 6th instead of the ♭7. The Dorian color, distilled.

  • Over m7 — pure Dorian without the modal commitment of the full scale
  • Over dom7 — on the 5th degree (D Dorian pentatonic over G7) (OS clip pentatonics · 00:30–00:35)

Dominant Pentatonic

1 · 2 · 3 · 5 · ♭7

Mixolydian, distilled. McCoy's primary color.

  • Native voice over dom7
  • Stack on the root and a half-step up (C & D♭ over a C pedal) (NK 2020-09-17 · 06:26–07:03; NK 2022-09-04 · 08:57–12:00)
  • Cycle: 1-3-♭7-2-5 → 2-5-1-3-♭7 →… (NK 2020-08-20 · 01:02–01:51)
  • Also taught with the bass deciding: one set of D dominant pentatonic voicings is D7, C6/9♯11, Am6 or F♯ø, depending on the note underneath (NK 2020-08-20 · 02:25–05:50)
  • The minor-pentatonic version is Kellman's pentatonic cycle in Reference

Altered Pentatonic

1 · ♭3 · 3 · ♭5 · ♭7

Tension scale for V7alt resolutions.

  • On ♭5 of dom7alt — D♭ altered pentatonic over G7alt
  • Pairs with hexatonic altered for thicker color

m6 (Coltrane) Pentatonic

1 · 2 · ♭3 · 5 · 6

A single shape that unlocks an entire Coltrane progression.

  • In root position: i6, VIIalt, IV9, vib5, ii7sus4♭9
  • On the ♭9 of 7alt — A♭ minor pentatonic over G7alt
  • Coltrane changes: i6 VIIalt | iii6 ♭IIIalt | bvi6 Valt

Blues Hexatonic (honorary pentatonic)

1 · ♭3 · 4 · ♭5 · 5 · ♭7

Six-note blues. Minor pentatonic plus the flat fifth — the blue note that does all the work.

  • Over any blues chord — I, IV, V; the key's blues scale over whole progressions is in What plays over what
  • The parent from which the two pentatonic distillations are carved

Pentatonic blues I

1 · ♭3 · 3 · 5 · 6

For the I chord in a blues. The ♭3-to-3 slur is the sound.

  • Over a major I in a blues — keeps the major tonality but with grit

Pentatonic blues IV

1 · ♭3 · 3 · 5 · ♭7

For the IV chord in a blues. The ♭7 carries the IV's dominant character.

  • Over the IV7 in a 12-bar blues

Lydian Dominant Pentatonic

1 · 3 · ♯4 · 6 · ♭7

The ♯4 and ♭7 together — lydian dominant in five notes.

  • Over tritone substitutions
  • Over dominants that aren't V–I (backdoor, secondary)

Cells, not scales

Play the dominant pentatonic in four-note cells — 1 2 3 5, 2 3 5 ♭7, 3 5 ♭7 1 — then reorder and chain them, and slide the cells a half step up and back. (NK 2020-09-17 · 02:09–07:03)

Permute one cell 1 2 3 5 → 2 3 5 1 → 3 2 5 1 Chain three 1 2 3 5 | 3 2 ♭7 1 | 5 ♭7 1 2 — up and down the keyboard Side-slip as on the Dominant Pentatonic card above

Three ways to stop it sounding like a scale: double-tap a note, pause, change direction mid-run. Fingering: in F, 1 2 3 1 3 | 1 2 3 1 3 (the jump from 3); on G♭ his own 1 2 3 4 | 1 2 3 4, because the F fingering is awkward there. (NK 2022-09-04 · 02:33–10:07)

Two zones for practising lines: C minor pentatonic over Cm7 with the thumb on C (C E♭ F G), then with the thumb on G (G B♭ C E♭). Run each zone up and down, make melodies inside one zone, then move between the zones freely; fourths in the left hand. (OS clip pentatonic lines · 00:05–00:56)

A scale loop: F minor pentatonic five notes down, start one note higher and five down again, and so on back up — one seamless line; then over Fm – A♭2 – D♭2 – B♭9sus – G♭∆7♯11. (OS clip maness warmup pentatonic exercise · 00:00–00:30)

Find a Mode

Search by sound or by name.

Type the accidentals you hear and get every mode containing them, closest color first — enharmonics fold together, so ♯4 and ♭5 return the same thing. Or type a name and get its accidentals, its family, and exactly where it sits in that family. Names accept nicknames (altered, acoustic, spanish), a root (F♯ dorian), or a coordinate (mode 4 of melodic minor). Pentatonics, hexatonics and the special scales are searched too, by name or by notes.

Find a Chord

Search by name or by notes.

Type a chord symbol and get its notes, its formula and every scale that fits it, best fit first. Or type the notes you hear and get the chord's name — every name, since the same notes often spell more than one chord. Standard and NewJazz spellings both work (Dm7♭5, Dmi7b5, CMa7, Cm∆7). For the common chord types with each scale explained, see What plays over what, just below.

Scales by Chord Type

What plays over what.

Every scale for each chord type, in C — the major-scale and blues options, then every melodic-minor and harmonic-minor mode that fits, each named with its parent, the harmonic-major and symmetric options from the NewJazz major and minor ii–V–i menus, then the pentatonics and hexatonics, including the NewJazz harmonic-minor hexatonic. For any other chord, search Find a Chord, just above. Each chord read as a mode is in The Chord Atlas. (NK 2021-03-04 · 02:36–14:42; NK 2021-03-11 · 04:21–15:47)

James Santangelo

Six notes, nine chords.

The first six tones of harmonic major — 1 to 5, plus the ♭6. One scale that re-interprets itself across an entire diatonic harmony, with every chord built on a different mode of the same six notes.

C Hexatonic Major

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · ♭6 · C · D · E · F · G · A♭

The scale itself. The chord chart below shows how this same set of six notes interprets nine distinct harmonies.

Degree Chord Chord, with C hexatonic Scale interpretation

So C hexatonic major (C D E F G A♭) sits over all of these at once: cleanly over Dm7♭5, Fm∆7, G7sus♭9, A♭∆7♯5 and B♭7♯11, and "sort of" over the altered-dominant and diminished readings. Any of the chords (like dom7♯9♯5) can work as a substitution.

The chain, in practice

The practical payoff: three hexatonics a fourth apart carry a whole minor ii–V–i, and each one reads as a different set of extensions over its chord.

A♭7♯11 with B♭ hex

B♭ C D E♭ F G♭ reads 9 · 3 · ♯11 · 5 · 13 · ♭7 — a complete Lydian-dominant colour with no root in the hand.

G7alt with E♭ hex

E♭ F G A♭ B♭ B reads ♭13 · ♭7 · 1 · ♭9 · ♯9 · 3 — six of the seven altered tones.

Cm∆7 with G hex

G A B C D E♭ reads 5 · 13 · 7 · 1 · 9 · ♭3 — the melodic-minor tonic, major 7th included.

A♭7♯11 with B♭ hex → G7alt with E♭ hex → Cm∆7 with G hex the hexatonics go up a fourth, then a major third The hand shape is identical each time; only where you put it changes.
The Barry Harris System

Sixth on the diminished.

One scale that alternates a sixth chord with a diminished seventh — and a way of hearing the whole ii–V as a single dominant. The bebop grammar underneath the notes.

The ii–V is one dominant.

Don't switch scales bar to bar — D Dorian for one measure, G Mixolydian for the next. Play one G-dominant sentence across the whole ii–V, and let the emphasis shift.

Over Dm7 emphasize

D · F · A · C

Relative to G7 these are the 5, ♭7, 9, 11 — the upper structure of the dominant.

Over G7 emphasize

B · D · F · A

The 3, 5, ♭7, 9. Then resolve: F→E and B→B (or C) into C∆7.

That's why the minor chord is just the dominant's upper structure: G7 = Dm6 over G (D F A B = 5, ♭7, 9, 3 → a G13).

The sixth-diminished scales

Eight notes alternating a sixth chord with a diminished seventh a tone up. Every other note belongs to the 6 chord; the notes between belong to the °7. Harmonize a melody by alternating inversions of the two — inner voices move while the tonic holds. (NK 2021-12-17 · 01:25–04:30; OS clip Barry Harris 6th Diminished Basics · 04:26–05:53)

Major-6 diminished

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · ♭6 · 6 · 7

C6 ↔ D°7. The tonic-major color with moving inner voices.

Minor-6 diminished

1 · 2 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 · ♭6 · 6 · 7

Cm6 ↔ D°7. Over a minor tonic — Cm6, Cm∆7, minor-blues i.

Dominant-7 diminished

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · ♭6 · ♭7 · 7

C7 ↔ D°7. Movement inside a dominant without going fully altered.

Two different dominant collections — don't conflate them. The dominant bebop scale (1 2 3 4 5 6 ♭7 7, with A natural) is for single-note lines. The dominant-7 diminished scale above (1 2 3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7 7, with A♭) is for harmonized C7↔D°7 movement and a stronger ♭13 color.

Practise the scale first in contrary motion, both hands from one note outward — in octaves, then in thirds: Barry Harris’s own first step, and the start of inner voices that land on the beat. (OS clip Barry Harris 6th Diminished Basics · 02:38–04:26)

Why the passing tone is there

The bebop scale's added note isn't decoration — it's metric alignment. Run C dominant bebop in eighth notes from a chord tone and the chord tones (C, E, G, B♭) land on the downbeats; the passing tones fill the offbeats. That alignment is what makes the line swing instead of drift. (NK 2021-12-17 · 05:52–08:21; OS clip Barry Harris 6th Diminished Basics · 00:39–02:15)

Major-6 dim aligns to a C6 (C–A–G–E on the beats); minor-6 dim to Cm6 (C–A–G–E♭). Same principle: structurally important notes on structurally important beats.

Surrounding & approach

Surround the target

Approach a chord tone from a half step above and below before landing. Apply to the tones of the tonic, the dominant 7, the diminished, and the important-minor chord.

Target B over G7: C – B♭ – B Target F over G7: G – E – F Target D over G7: E – C♯ – D

Diminished over ♭9

A♭°7 over G7♭9 · A♭ · B · D · F

A♭ = ♭9, B = 3, D = 5, F = ♭7. Symmetric — start the same arpeggio from any of its four notes for a new contour.

Also taught as a family of four dominants over one bass: B°7 over G is G7♭9; lower one of its notes a half step at a time and the same hand becomes B♭7 (♯9 ♭9), D♭7 (♯11 ♭9) and E7 (13 ♭9) over G. The rule behind it is in the Reference block Diminished System for Dominants. (NK 2021-12-17 · 11:01–14:42)

Two voices from one scale

Every note of the E♭ sixth-diminished scale belongs to one of its two chords — the E♭6 or the F°7. Harmonize a melody note with any other note of the same chord and the second voice is always right: in parallel, in contrary motion, or switching direction at will. (OS clip 6th Diminished Workout · 05:07–17:19)

SetNotesA melody note here takes
E♭6 — the tonicE♭ · G · B♭ · Cany other of E♭ G B♭ C
F°7 — the dominant (B♭7♭9 without its root)F · A♭ · B · Dany other of F A♭ B D
1 Parallel — the same distance under the melody, chosen inside the set 2 Contrary — start on a shared note and move out as the melody moves 3 Free — switch direction whenever the line wants to 4 The same scale covers Cm7, the relative minor, and Dø – G7 into it 5 At the IV (B♭m7 in E♭) switch to the A♭ sixth-diminished

Worked on the first four bars of “There Will Never Be Another You”. In this way of hearing, a minor 7th is a 6 chord with the 6 in the bass, and a ii–V–I is really V–I, so one sixth-diminished scale carries the cadence; each melody note can bring its own small tension or rest.

The Blues

Twelve bars, eight ways.

Eight harmonizations of the same form — playable, in C — plus the passing chords that connect them, the guide tones that steer them, and the Barry-Harris language for soloing over them. The blues collections themselves live up in Pentatonics, and the hand-shape approach — blues as grips rather than scales — is in NewJazz.

The blues lab — eight charts, all in C

The same form, harmonized eight ways: three chords, then a jazz blues, then a substitution chorus, then a full reharmonization. Click any chord to hear it. Press play to run the chorus in time — the bar you're in lights up.

Hear it in blocks of four

Don't memorize twelve bars. Memorize three four-bar sentences — each one ends with a ii–V pointing somewhere.

Bars 1–4 · home & the IV

C7 · F7 · C7 · Gm7 – C7

Statement, the quick change to IV, back home. The bar-4 Gm7–C7 is a ii–V in F — it exists only to deliver you to the IV chord.

Bars 5–8 · the IV & the pivot

F7 · F♯°7 · C7 · Em7 – A7♭9

The ♯IV°7 in bar 6 walks you back. Bar 8's Em7–A7♭9 is a ii–V in D minor — aiming at the Dm7 in bar 9.

Bars 9–12 · the cadence

Dm7 · G7 · C7 – A7♭9 · Dm7 – G7alt

A ii–V in C, resolving in bar 11 — then an I–VI–ii–V turnaround throws you back to the top.

Learn the numeric sequence first. Play the whole form with left-hand voicings, eyes closed. Only then start improvising over it.

Guide tones steer it

The 3rd and ♭7 of each dominant define the changes. Voice-lead them and the blues plays itself: every move is a half step.

Chord3rd♭7
C7EB♭
F7AE♭
G7BF

C7 → F7 resolution

E → E♭ and B♭ → A, both down a half step. Going back F7 → C7, run it in reverse.

Getting from I to IV

Almost every blues reharmonization is a different answer to one question: what do you play in the beat and a half between C7 and F7? Six answers, all interchangeable.

Tritone slide

C7 → G♭7 → F7

The ♭II7 of F — a half step above the target, so both guide tones fall by a semitone. The single most-used passing chord in New Orleans playing.

Augmented dominant

C7♯5 → F7  ·  C → G+7 → C9 → F7

Raise the 5th of the I7 and the G♯ pulls up into A — the 3rd of F7. The same trick backwards: a G+7 over a C bass makes the tonic itch to move.

Sus, then a half step

C7sus4 → E7 → F7

Suspend, then approach the IV from a half step below. Swap the E7 for a G♭7 and you approach from above instead — same device, opposite direction.

C7sus4 · E7 · F7 from below C7sus4 · G♭7 · F7 from above

The walk-up

C7 · Dm7 · E♭°7 · C7/E → F7

One chord per beat, bass climbing C–D–E♭–E into F. The E♭°7 is just a chromatic connector between the ii and the first inversion of the I. (OS clip OS walkup walkdown · 00:00–00:26)

The backdoor

F7 → Fm7 – B♭7 → C

Coming home from the IV: minor it, add the ♭VII7, and B♭7's ♭7 (A♭) falls to G while its 3rd (D) sits under the C. Gospel's favorite return.

Oscar Peterson’s dominant chain

G7 → B7 – E7 – A7 – D7 → G

In a G blues, after the return to I: III7, VI7, II7, V7, each the dominant of the next, round to G. The ending goes D7 → A♭7(13) → G13(♯11 ♭9), a tritone-sub approach. (OS clip osj oscarpeterson blues · 00:15–00:53)

The ♯IV°7

F7 → F♯°7 → C7/G

The bar-6 chord. F♯→G in the bass, E♭→E on top. It's also a rootless D7♭9 — which is why bar 6 can become a ii–V into the second half.

Also taught as ten ways from C to F, adding to these: C/E or E7 underneath; the ♭III, E♭, straight into F; D♭ – E♭ – F; a diatonic or a whole-step walk-down; “a couple of perfects”, G7 – C7 – F; and “a couple of plagals”, E♭ – B♭ – F. (OS clip I to IV · 00:00–01:56)

Chord-tone soloing, in three passes

A good blues solo is roughly 85% chord tones. Everything else — the chromaticism, the blue notes, the bebop scale — is the route between them. Build it in this order and don't skip ahead.

Pass 1 — chord tones only. 1 · 3 · 5 · ♭7 of whatever chord you're on. Nothing else. Boring is the point. Pass 2 — approach & enclosure. Surround each target from above and below before you land on it. Pass 3 — passing tones. Now the bebop scale, the ♭3→3 crush, and the chromatic fill.

Targets through the first five bars

Bar 1 C7 land on E (the 3rd) Bar 2 F7 land on E♭ (½ step down) Bar 3 C7 land on B♭ (the ♭7) Bar 4 Gm7–C7 aim at A (3rd of the F7 ahead) Bar 5 F7 land on A

Decide the arrival note before you play the phrase. Then choose a route to it.

Enclose the target

Target E over C7: F – E♭ – E Target A over F7: B♭ – G♯ – A Target B♭ over C7: B – C – B♭ Target B over G7: C – B♭ – B

Above, below, land. Reverse it, double it, or make the upper note diatonic and the lower one chromatic — the shape survives.

Also taught as patterns into the 5 of C7: 13 → ♯11 → ♭13 → ♯11 → 5, or start on the ♯11 and circle the 5 (F♯ A A♭ A A♭ F♯ G, read from his keys). Move a pattern to the ♭7 or the 3, but not around the root, where it clashes; then chain cells around one chord tone after another. (NK 2021-09-04 · 02:40–06:43)

The same job approached as hand shapes rather than target notes is in NewJazz: the three-finger engine and the 1 ♭3 4 8 climb, four positions over one dominant that carry you out and back in.

Straight, No Chaser is this form with a single rhythmic cell displaced across it. Play the head, take the second chorus, and develop one motif rather than eleven ideas.

Left hand: tenths and a walking line

The stride-and-New-Orleans left hand: root and 3rd split by a tenth, chromatic connectors between them. Play these under a right hand that's doing nothing at all — then add the solo.

Tenths through the I

Root in the bass, 3rd a tenth above. Break it — bass on beat 1, the tenth on beat 2 — and the harmony walks itself.

C · E♭°7 – G7 · C7 – Gm7 C7 – G♭7 · F7 – G♭7 · F7

Chromatic walking bass

Two eight-bar choruses. Every chord is one or two beats; the bass connects them by half step wherever it can.

C Am7 | Gm7 F♯7 | F7 | B♭9 C/G A+7 | D7 G7 | Em7 E♭7 | Dm7 D♭13 C Am7 | Gm7 C7♯9♯5 | F6 | Fm6 C/G A+7 | A♭13 G9 | Em7 A7 | D7♭5 G7♯9♯5

Emmet Cohen’s solo-blues left hand: legato and steady — octaves or rolled tenths with pedal — steady enough to send a text message while it runs, which frees the right hand. In B♭, I → IV in one bar from above via E (E7, or E7 – E♭7 – E° – B♭/F) or from below via D; and the church walk-up B♭ – Cm – C° – B♭/D. (OS clip Emmett Cohen Blues · 00:00–07:52)

Barry over the embedded ii–V's

Each little ii–V is one dominant environment (see Barry Harris). The minor chord is just the dominant's upper structure.

Gm7 – C7 → play C dominant (sets up F7) Dm7 – G7 → play G dominant (sets up C7) Em7 – A7 → play A dominant (sets up Dm7)

And run dominant bebop straight over the I, IV, and V — C bebop over C7, F over F7, G over G7. Don't switch on beat 1; anticipate the next dominant on the & of 4, or let the line spill a beat past the bar line (delayed resolution). Both keep it from sounding square.

Diminished & the blue third

The ♯IV°7 (bar 6)

F♯°7 · F♯ · A · C · E♭

Resolve F♯→G, E♭→E, and you're back on C7. The same symmetric arpeggio works from any of its four notes.

The ♭3 → 3 crush

E♭ slurred into E over C7

The blue note. Grace it, repeat it, or trill it into the major 3rd. Over F7 the E♭ becomes the chord's ♭7 — let it sit. Back on C7, E natural is the target again.

A 12-bar blues, made modern

Four ways to modernise an F blues without losing the form. Playing out works when it leads to a resolution; the sus substitutes sit best with a bassist holding the roots. (NK 2020-11-27 · 01:08–08:08)

1 Solo in the Mixolydian a tritone away — B over F7, E over B♭7, F♯ over C7 — and resolve back (B → B♭ Mixolydian on the B♭7) — the general rule is in Dissonance formulas 2 Make every dominant a 13sus, 1 ♭7 9 4 13: F13sus, B♭13sus, G13sus, C13sus (read from his keys) 3 Replace the second chord of each four-bar phrase with the chord a half step above the first: F7 → F♯7, B♭7 → B7, Gm7 → A♭m/C 4 McCoy Tyner: an open fifth in the left hand plus F sus fourths (F B♭ E♭), moved up a half step or in whole steps; F dominant pentatonic in the right

Blues riffs under the fingers

Riffs in F built from finger groups, slides and trills. Most rely on black keys moving to white, so other keys need their own fingerings. (NK 2021-01-14 · 01:30–08:13; NK 2022-06-07 · 01:12–09:43)

Gospel

Sunday morning, from a jazz chair.

Church harmony as a jazz pianist uses it: a major scale that leaves out its major 7th, chords approached from a half step below, pathways between I, IV, ii, V and vi, and the small habits — the dominant walk-up, the V played as a sus, the grace note into the middle voice — that carry the sound. The scale itself lives in What plays over what.

Approach chords, from a half step below

Five targets in B♭, each reached from a half step below and slid into. The moo chord — 1 2 5 over its own 3rd — is the usual approach; a ♯9 dominant is the other. (OS clip osj gospel hour · 08:18–17:29)

TargetApproach → arrivalVoicing
IV · E♭D7♯9 → E♭∆9 (no 3rd)D octave | F♯ C F (3 ♭7 ♯9) → E♭ B♭ | F B♭ D — a B♭ triad over E♭: 1 5 | 9 5 7
ii · CmG(2)/B → Cm11G A D over B → C | F B♭ E♭ — the 11 takes the 5th's place; all fourths
IV · E♭B♭(2)/D → E♭∆7melody on the 3rd; a G minor triad over E♭
V · FC(2)/E → F13sus4F | D E♭ B♭ — 13, ♭7, and the 4 on top
vi · GmD(2)/F♯ → Gm11a wider minor 11 with an F major triad inside

Over the D7♯9, improvise with D altered — or hear it as A♭ Lydian dominant, the tritone away: the same notes. The half-step move in a standard is Passing chords a half step away; the moo itself is defined under the moo chord warmup.

Also taught in G: B7(♯9♭13) up to C∆7, then F13♯11; and a dominant III in the 3–6–2–5 — B7(♯9♭13) – Em11 – A7 – D7sus4 – G. (OS clip maness gospel · 00:17–00:50)

Pathways between the chords

Know where you start and where you are going, then take the scenic route: six short paths, all inside the Sunday scale except where a chord says otherwise. (OS clip OS gospel pathways · 00:00–18:20)

One melody, three settings

The same melody in B♭, harmonized three ways. Each setting keeps the tune and changes only what sits under it, ending on the IV. (OS clip osj gospel hour · 21:25–44:47)

Setting 1 Cm7 (= E♭/C) – B♭ – Cm – B♭ – E♭ – B♭ – E♭ – B♭ | Gm7 – C7 – Fm7 – B♭7 – E♭ Setting 2 Cm7 – B♭ – E♭6 – B♭ – E♭∆7 – B♭(2)/D – Cm7 – B♭ | Gm7 – D(2)/F♯ – Fm9 – D7♯9 – E♭∆9 (no 3rd) Setting 3 Cm11 – B♭(2)/D – E♭∆7 – B♭(2)/D – G(2)/B – Cm11 – A°7 – D(2)/F♯ – Gm7 – D(2)/F♯ – Fm9 – D7♯9 – E♭∆9 (no 3rd)

Setting 1 is triads over a left-hand line from the Sunday scale, the iii–VI–ii–V as root, shell and melody. Setting 2 lets the bass rise against the melody: E♭6 is a C minor triad over E♭, E♭∆7 a G minor triad over E♭, and the iii walks down to the IV through a moo and the ♯9 approach. Setting 3 adds the spread minor 11, chains of moos, and A°7 – D(2)/F♯ – Gm7 as a longer approach to the relative minor.

Also taught in five levels on one 3/4 melody — root only; triads; approach chords; moos and polychords in a two-feel; then “big church” (D♭7♯9♯11 – C13sus – E°7 – Gm, A♭∆9 without its 3rd). (OS clip OS gospel sunday school · 00:00–31:00)

The cliches, used sparingly

Five habits that make the sound — each one corny if it is everywhere, so choose the spots. (OS clip OS gospel cliches · 00:00–13:37)

ClicheHow
Dominant walk-upsitting on V in B♭: F7 – Gm7 – A♭°7 – F/A, in tenths; diatonic, plus the bluesy ♭3 and ♭5
The V as a susii – E♭/F – I: a triad over the 5 instead of a plain dominant — no 3rd, so the Sunday scale holds
IV from its 3rdin G: G – G/B or B7♯9♭13 – C, a half step below the IV
The grace notea diatonic grace into the second-from-top note of a triad (B♭ → C inside a C minor triad); on top it turns melodic and bluesy — ♭3 → 3, ♭5 → 5
Octaveshigh, on the tonic, in simple rhythms played with authority; low, under the dominant walk-up
Modal Interchange / Chromatic Mediants

Borrow a brighter key.

Reharmonize every chord in a progression — all but the I — into a key a third away. The tonic stays home; everything around it gets relit in a neighboring tonality. (OS clip maness up m3 · 00:00–00:30; OS clip maness warmup modal interchange1 · 00:00–00:38)

Major 3rd above

C → E

Reharmonize into the key a natural third up. Bright, lifting. C∆7 and E∆7 share only one tone — B — which is what makes the shift feel like a lit window.

Major 3rd below

C → A♭

Down a natural third. Warm, flattening. A♭∆7's major 7th is G — the 5th of C — so it settles rather than lifts.

Minor 3rd above

C → E♭

Up a minor third — relative-major shimmer. Apply it twice — C, then the E♭ family, then the G♭ family — always returning to the C tonic. (OS clip maness warmup modal interchange2 · 00:00–00:46)

Minor 3rd below

C → A

Down a minor third — toward the relative minor's brightness.

Melodic minor m3 below

C → A melodic minor

A minor third below, but borrowing melodic minor instead of major.

So What interchange

Dm7 → F♯m7 · B♭m7

Transpose a minor chord up major thirds. The modal-interchange staple — especially over modal tunes like So What.

The flip

Am7 · G7 → Cm

Turn the game around: the tonic goes minor and everything else stays in the major key — vi–V–I as Am7 – G7 – Cm, I–ii–iii–IV as Cm – Dm – Em – F. (OS clip Modal interchange · 00:22–01:35)

Beyond Dorian

D minor: i · v · ♭VI · iv

In a minor key the mode shows in the v chord. Over Dm7 – v – B♭∆7 – Gm7: Am11 (Aeolian), A7♭9 (harmonic minor — B♭ and C♯), Am7♭5 (Phrygian — the ♭2, E♭). (OS clip osj maness beyond dorian · 00:00–00:43)

The general move: slide the key up or down a minor third or major third across any chord progression, leaving the tonic in place. Each destination recolors the same harmonic function with a different parent scale.

Also taught chord by chord rather than key by key, as a Ravel habit: the bass moves a major or minor third between chord types — a half-diminished chord to the m6 or the 6 chord a major third up, dominants falling by thirds (B♭7 → G♭7 → E♭7 → C7), C7 to Eø a major third up. (NK 2022-04-24 · 20:06–24:17)

Also taught as one progression three ways: C – G – Am – F – C/E – Dm7 – G7sus; in minor Cm – Gm7 – A♭ – Fm – Cm/E♭ – Dm7♭5 – G7♭9sus; then mixed, each chord from whichever key colours it: C – Gm7 – A♭∆7 – F – Cm/E♭ – Dm7 – G7♭9sus. (OS clip chord progressions · 00:00–00:47)

Also taught chord by chord as a composer’s drill: C → E → A♭ in one rhythm, then in minor, Cm → Em → A♭m. Two minor chords a major third apart make a sound of their own — Cm with Gm/B♭ and E♭ from its key, Em with C∆7 from its own. (OS clip chromatic mediants · 00:00–00:45; OS clip osj radiohead inlimbo · 00:00–00:59)

Triad + 1

Three notes plus one.

A triad with one added color tone, voiced through every inversion. The simplest melodic device with the deepest grammar.

Triad + 1 (C maj + 9)

C · D · E · G

Take any triad, add one extension — here the 9 — and use every inversion of the four-note shape.

  • C D E G · D E G C · E G C D · G C D E
  • Works on any triad with any extension (9, 11, 13, +5, etc.)
  • Also taught with the 4: F major + 4 (C F A B♭) as a right-hand ostinato cell and as one hand of a two-hand arpeggio; and as a tonic, Csus4/add4 — a triad plus 4, not a 7sus4 (NK 2021-04-01 · 06:39–08:25; NK 2023-03-01 · 03:51–04:29; NK 2021-02-18 · 14:44–16:15)

Playing Out with Triads

C/E + E♭m/B♭ · two inversions, two chords

Use any two triads — provided they're in two different inversions and from two separate chords.

  • e.g., C 1st inversion (E G C) + E♭m 2nd inversion (B♭ E♭ G♭)
  • The inversion mismatch is what makes it sound deliberate, not random
  • Slide either triad chromatically and resolve

Two major triads over a progression: the triad-pair lesson is in NewJazz, with the Barry Harris reading in The Barry Harris System.

Two triads, one voicing

Stack two triads and the pair is a voicing. Keep the lower triad, change the upper one, and log what you hear — D/C is C6/9♯11, B/C is C∆7♯9♯11, B minor over C minor is Cm(∆9)♯11. Voice-led pairs move in fourths: D/C → G/F → C/B♭, with D in 2nd inversion over C, then G in 1st over F in 2nd. (NK 2022-02-06 · 01:49–14:07)

Upper Structures

A triad over a dominant.

Put the chord's root, 3rd and ♭7 in the left hand. Stack a plain major triad on top with the right. The triad you choose names the extension — one familiar shape spelling a 13♯11, a 7♯9, a fully altered chord. Shown over C7.

Voicings by chord type

Shapes for particular chord colours, as Kellman voices them; each chord read as a mode stays in The Chord Atlas. The triad-over-dominant cards follow below.

The diminished-major seventh

A diminished triad with a major 7th — 1 ♭3 ♭5 7 — is a working chord: it delays a landing, replaces a plain °7 on a half-step descent, and sits a half step from the chord it resolves to. Every note of it is in the whole-half diminished scale on its root. (NK 2023-01-24 · 06:31–08:15; NK 2022-05-01 · 01:04–02:39)

A♭°∆7 over F → F∆ delay the landing on I Em → E♭°∆7 → Dm instead of a plain E♭°7 (E♭ F♯ A D) D♭°∆7 → D♭∆ before the tonic — like C7 over D♭ E♭°9(∆7) 1 9 ♭3 ♭5 7 a cluster: E♭ F F♯ A D F°∆7 up in minor thirds a left-hand pattern

Also: (NK 2023-07-29 · 10:36–11:04; NK 2020-12-10 · 06:16–07:08; NK 2022-05-01 · 05:18–06:01). As a block chord it is in Seventh block chords.

Clusters with one doubled note

Rolled and high, a cluster rings when one note — usually the 9 — is doubled; doubling more than one weakens it. Name a cluster so the reader plays it as meant, and try it over other bass notes. (NK 2021-09-26 · 01:06–06:27; NK 2020-12-10 · 00:51–07:45)

♭13 · 1 · ♯9 — fully altered

The pattern: name the triad by where its root sits over the chord. A triad on the 9 (II) and one on the ♭7 (♭VII) keep things consonant; triads on the ♭VI, ♭V and VI pull into altered territory. The two unaltered ones (II, ♭VII) belong over a V going anywhere; the altered ones want a V resolving down a fifth to a tonic.

Also taught between a sus and its resolution: F13sus → D/F7 (the VI card) or B/F7 (the ♭V card) → B♭∆7. (OS clip osj sus chord triads · 00:00–01:18)

Over a major chord the move is gentler — II major over C∆7 gives 9·♯11·13 (the Lydian color from the Triad + 1 page), and iii minor (Em) is just C∆7's own 3-5-7. Over minor, a major triad up a ♭7 (B♭ over Cm) voices Cm11. (NK 2022-02-06 · 01:49–03:50; NK 2020-08-06 · 02:48–03:29)

A five-note set for every chord family, the altered one built on these triads: see the Magic Voicing System in Comping.

One minor-11 shape, any root

Kellman's most-used voicing is one minor 11 — 1 5 9 ♭3 11 ♭7, an open fifth under a cluster — and he treats it as a hand shape to move, not a chord to spell. Practise it by half steps, whole steps, minor and major thirds, fourths and fifths; the minor-third motion is the modern sound he credits to Robert Glasper. (NK 2021-07-03 · 01:03–04:36; NK 2020-06-11 · 02:33–03:11)

Arpeggios

Voicings, set in motion.

An arpeggio here is a voicing played one note at a time — so the same upper structures, rootless shapes and two-hand grips as everywhere else on the page, spread across the keyboard. Most of what follows is Noah Kellman’s: his formulas, his shapes, his two-hand cells, and his method for making your own. The keyboards play each one in order. Shapes are in C unless the source plays them in another key.

Four rootless formulas: ♭7 and 1 below, four notes above

The left hand plays the 7th and the root; the right hand plays an upper structure — the 9th, 3rd, ♯11 and 13 for a dominant or major chord, 9 ♭3 11 13 for a minor — and the arpeggio runs from the bottom up.

C13♯11 · dominant

LH ♭7 1 · RH 9 3 ♯11 13

B♭ C | D E F♯ A — Lydian dominant from the bottom up.

LH ♭7 1 · RH ♭9 3 ♯11 13

D♭ for D: the half-whole diminished colour.

C∆13♯11 · major

LH 7 1 · RH 9 3 ♯11 13

B in the left hand instead of B♭ — the same right hand, now Lydian.

Cm13 · minor

LH ♭7 1 · RH 9 ♭3 11 13

D E♭ F A — Dorian.

Making your own

Build an arpeggio from a voicing’s shapes: two four-note cells per octave, then a third, descending shape. Split it between the hands — 3 + 3, or 2 + 4 — or cross them, the right hand starting below where the left ended, for a Ravel or Debussy wash. (NK 2021-09-12 · 02:03–13:35; NK 2021-09-19 · 01:27–06:55)

Arpeggios elsewhere on the page: Herbie Hancock’s three on Stella; three arpeggios on one dominant (diminished, whole tone, altered) in What plays over what; the ballad arpeggio from a four-note voicing (E A B D over C) in Warmups; triad-pair lines and wide arpeggios in The triad pairs.

Playing Out

Leave the key on purpose.

Following the approach taught by Justin Highland, repeat one short pattern through a cycle of temporary centers: three on an augmented triad (the 3-tonic system), four on a diminished-seventh arpeggio (4-tonic), six on a whole-tone scale (6-tonic), eight on a diminished scale (8-tonic). Move the same intervals and rhythm to each stop, adapting the fingering as needed; the repetition makes the journey audible, and a clear landing brings it home. The cycle fixes the centers, not every note — how far out it sounds depends on the pattern and the harmony underneath.

What makes an outside line sound intentional isn't which notes you leave on — it's that the listener can hear the same shape arriving again. Symmetry supplies the pattern; the pattern supplies the permission.

The five divisions

Four tonic systems, with two versions of the 8-tonic. The 3-, 4- and 6-tonic cycles move in equal steps; the 8-tonic cycles alternate whole and half steps. The count is how many centers you visit before the cycle returns home.

Three words first. Tonality a temporary home note. You play your shape as if that note were the key. Step the distance from one tonality to the next. Cycle an ordered collection of centers. Equal steps give 3, 4 or 6 stops; alternating whole and half steps give 8. Return to the first center to close it.

Read each row left to right: choose the cycle, then move the same pattern to each center, keeping its intervals and rhythm. C is the starting center here; it need not be the bass or the chord root. Both 8-tonic rows contain C E♭ G♭ A, with one extra center between each pair. The tabs below play each cycle with a shape of your choice.

3 · 4 · 6 · 8 in practice

One worked route per system, starting on C.

3-tonic · augmented-triad centers Play the pattern in C, then E, then A♭ (G♯), then back to C. Any shape works. 4-tonic · diminished-seventh centers 5–1–2, each center as 1: C: G C D → E♭: B♭ E♭ F → G♭: D♭ G♭ A♭ → A: E A B → C 6-tonic · whole-tone centers A dominant-7 arpeggio at each center: C7 → D7 → E7 → F♯7 → G♯7 → B♭7. 1–3–5–♭7 puts a perfect fifth outside the whole-tone collection at every stop; 1–3–♯5–♭7 stays inside it. 8-tonic · diminished-scale centers Whole–half: C D E♭ F G♭ A♭ A B → C Half–whole: C D♭ E♭ E G♭ G A B♭ → C

Three destinations, connecting triads

A practice chain through the descending major-third destinations B → G → E♭ → B, with a minor triad between each pair: the minor triads connect the destinations rather than adding new ones. (user description)

B major → A minor → G major → F minor → E♭ major → D♭ minor → B major B D♯ F♯ → A C E → G B D → F A♭ C → E♭ G B♭ → D♭ F♭ A♭ → B D♯ F♯

Also taught as three familiar keys a major third apart — B, G, E♭ — each reached first by its V–I, then by its ii–V. (OS clip artweplay coltrane changes · 00:00–00:59)

D♭ minor is C♯ minor (C♯ E G♯), the ii of B. With sevenths and dominants the chain becomes three ii–V–I cells — Am7–D7–G∆7 · Fm7–B♭7–E♭∆7 · C♯m7–F♯7–B∆7 — the Coltrane-changes layout (this page's reading).

How each one behaves

Up in major thirds · 3

C → E → A♭

Three centers on an augmented triad. The major-third geometry behind Coltrane changes, which add dominant approaches between the centers — see Three destinations, connecting triads above. (NK 2021-01-07 · 08:01–09:16)

  • Over a major chord or tonic vamp; then connect the centers with ii–V approaches
  • Union of the three triads is the augmented scale
  • Three stops before the return — the shortest cycle to learn

Up in minor thirds · 4

C → E♭ → G♭ → A

Four centers on C°7 — 5–1–2 at each is worked out in 3 · 4 · 6 · 8 in practice. A pattern taken from one diminished scale stays in it all the way round. For the rootless C7♭9 arpeggio, start from D♭: D♭ → E → G → B♭. (NK 2020-12-31 · 01:18–08:16)

  • Over a V chord, with a pattern and starting center that fit it
  • Four stops, all chord tones of the same °7
  • Also taught with a 7sus resolving to its ∆7 (D♭7sus4 → G♭∆7), the pair moved round the circle of fourths, by tritones, or down in minor thirds (OS clip openstudio2 · 00:00–01:21)
  • Pairs with the diminished material in Special Scales

Whole tone · 6

C → D → E → F♯ → G♯ → B♭

Six centers, every other chromatic note. Augmented triads and 7♯5 arpeggios stay inside one whole-tone collection; major triads and plain dominant 7ths add notes outside it.

  • The whole-tone scale has no perfect fifths — pick a pattern without them to keep that sound
  • Six stops is a long trip; exit early if you need to
  • Resolve to a chord tone of the underlying harmony

Whole–half diminished · 8

C D E♭ F G♭ A♭ A B

Eight centers alternating whole step, half step. Denser than the minor-third cycle and it includes it — the °7 tones plus a passing tone between each. Diminished and tonic-diminished contexts.

  • Contains the minor-thirds cycle inside it
  • Alternating step sizes make the motion audible
  • Use over a °7 or a tonic-minor with movement

Half–whole diminished · 8

C D♭ E♭ E G♭ G A B♭

The dominant one. Against C7 these eight centers spell 1 ♭9 ♯9 3 ♯11 5 13 ♭7 — every center is a chord tone or a tension of the chord.

  • The furthest-out cycle: eight stops
  • Over a dominant 7 with ♭9 / ♯9 / 13
  • Start on the ♭9 or ♯11 to get out fast

Choosing the dial

At the same length per stop, fewer centers return home sooner. Pick the cycle, and how many stops to play, by the time you have; the timings below are practice suggestions.

2 bars → major 3rds 4 bars → minor 3rds 8 bars → whole tone or diminished

Working the system

1 Play a short shape in the home key — four or five notes, one bar or less. 2 Repeat it at the next center in the cycle. Same intervals and rhythm; adapt the fingering. 3 Keep the rhythm identical at every stop. The rhythm is what tells the listener it's a pattern. 4 Travel as far as the harmony gives you time for. You don't have to complete the cycle. 5 Exit by half step into a chord tone of the chord you're actually on. 6 Leave space immediately after. The silence confirms it was a choice.

Step 3 is the one people skip, and it's the one that does the work. Change the rhythm as you transpose and the whole thing collapses back into sounding lost. Step 5 is the other: an outside line is judged entirely by how it lands, and a half step into a 3rd or a ♭7 forgives almost anything that came before it. The Playing out tab in the ii–V–I lab applies this to a cadence, and the two-triad device in Triads & Upper Structures is the same principle with a smaller shape. (NK 2021-01-07 · 02:18–04:10)

Dissonance formulas: out on purpose

The divisions above move one shape through symmetric stops. A dissonance formula is a single superimposition you come back to — a scale or a chord over a chord it doesn't belong to — learned until you hear it, and always resolved. (NK 2021-02-18 · 02:24–04:37; NK 2021-07-06 · 00:48–01:36)

Sources for the rows: (NK 2021-02-04 · 02:57–06:56; NK 2023-03-19 · 01:33–02:00; NK 2022-07-24 · 14:58–16:51; NK 2020-11-27 · 01:08–03:28; NK 2021-02-18 · 04:37–12:38). The keyboard is his A♭m9 cluster over B♭7.

Also taught from the voicing side: any voicing you play on the V, moved up a half step, is a voicing of the II dominant. Hold the V in the bass under it, then resolve — A7♭9/D → D7♭9 → Gm in G minor, or the ♯9♯5 shape up a half step over D (written E♭7♯9♯5/D) → D7♯9; it works in major too. (OS clip ii-v-i · 00:30–01:28)

Resolution quizzing

An outside line is judged by how it lands, so practise the landing. With a metronome, improvise in one formula using bebop language — approach notes, enclosures — then resolve into the home key; if the landing doesn't convince you, stop, recall what you did, and find a better route. (NK 2023-03-19 · 02:13–04:08)

1 Two bars of the formula (E major over C), then resolve to C — free time first, then 80 bpm 2 Judge the landing: an enclosure onto the 3 can feel cheap; three notes of C Lydian lead in better 3 Start the resolving line a few notes early, before the chord arrives 4 Harder: two beats out, two beats in, alternating 5 Invent your own formulas — one scale over another, only ones you like

The same lean ahead is a drill of its own: start the next chord's scale a beat, two beats, a whole chord early — see Anticipate in Time & Phrasing. (NK 2023-03-19 · 04:27–08:58)

NewJazz · Oliver Prehn

Three grips, and the bass decides.

A complete left-hand chord system built from three grips. The grips are upper structures — some include the keynote, and the bass player supplies the low foundation, or you cross over with the right hand to practise. The grips never change; what changes is the note underneath, and that alone turns one grip into a minor 9, a 13sus, an altered dominant or a minor 6/9. (NJ 2018-05a · 01:01; NJ 2018-06 · 01:00; NJ 2018-07a · 00:00; NJ 2019-12 · 01:27)

The same grip, with a different bass, is a different chord. Learn two inversions of Grip 1, two of Grip 2, one of Grip 3 — and you can voice nearly every chord in a standard without ever learning a voicing per chord.

Voicing audit · v3.7: a chord family is not always a complete chord spelling. Grip 2 over a half-diminished bass gives 1, 11, ♭5, ♭7 but omits ♭3; add the minor third for a complete ø7, or hear it as 7sus4♭5. Minor 6/9 grips omit the major 7; major 6/9 grips omit the major 7 too. The row supplies these tones only when they are actually played. Position 2 alone does not supply B in the C-melodic-minor examples; the F13♯11 and Cm∆7 demonstrations now add B explicitly.

The three grips

Grip 1 and Grip 2 each get two inversions, named a and b, so progressions stay smooth without leaping. Grip 3 is played in one inversion only. (NJ 2018-05a · 03:08; NJ 2018-06 · 02:05; NJ 2018-07a · 23:34) Grips 4a, 4b and 5, below the line, are not NewJazz’s: they extend the numbering with three more rootless shapes. (user description) Grip 4a is 3 · 6 · 9 over a dominant with 1 · ♭7 in the left hand, as in the Mountain warmup (OS note opstIG1); Kellman voices a dominant the same way (NK 2022-12-18 · 03:29–04:42) and uses the same shape over a major chord (C6/9) (NK 2020-09-03 · 01:35).

Why inversions

Two inversions per grip is enough to move anywhere without the hand jumping. Play 1a→2a in one register and 1b→2b in the other; pick whichever keeps you near where you already are.

Grip 4 · 4a

C F B♭. Put it on the 3rd of a dominant with 1 and ♭7 in the left hand: A D G over F E♭ is F13 (3 · 13 · 9).

Grip 4 · 4b

C D G — grip 2a without its bottom note: 2a on A♭ is A♭ C D G; drop the A♭. Over B♭ it is 9 · 3 · 13. Because it is 2a minus one note, the chain below simply uses 2a.

Grip 5

C E♭ G B♭ — a minor-7th shape. On the 3rd of a major chord it is the rootless major 9th: G B♭ D F over E♭ is E♭∆9.

Same job — the chord’s 3 · 5 · 7 · 9 with no root — in opposite shapes: drop the root from a minor 9th and a major-7th shape is left; drop it from a major 9th and a minor-7th shape is left. Grip 5 is also the rootless C∆9 (E G B D) in Comping; 4a is the right hand of the Mountain warmup (3 · 6 · 9 over 1 · ♭7). The chain that uses all three is Grips 4a, 4b and 5 round the circle of fifths, after the core progression.

Grip 1: move the bass a fifth, change everything

The cleanest demonstration in the system. One grip, two bass notes a fifth apart, two unrelated-sounding chords. (NJ 2018-05a · 15:49)

Bass a m3 below · minor 9

E♭ G B♭ D over C = ♭3 5 ♭7 9 — Cm9.

Bass a m7 below · 13sus

The identical grip over F = ♭7 9 11 13 — F13sus. The bass simply fell a fifth.

Also taught as a right-hand trick: keep the ii's arpeggio while the bass moves to the V. Dm7 over G gives G7 sus2 sus4; Dm9 over G adds the 6 (sus2 sus4 sus6); in minor, Dm7♭5 over G gives G7 sus♭2 sus4, usually written G7♭9sus4. Resolve it or leave it hanging. (NJ 2023-11b · 11:40)

Also taught as a substitution rule: keep the ii's minor 9 over the V's bass — Gm9 over C is C13sus, 1 4 5 ♭7 9 13 — then make every dominant of a blues a 13sus: Cm9/F, Fm9/B♭, Gm9/C. (NK 2022-09-25 · 03:35–10:35; NK 2020-11-27 · 04:12–05:46)

Grip 2: four chord qualities from one grip

Run a sequence of fifths alternating 2b and 2a, attach a different family of bass notes each time, and the same hand produces four different chord types in all twelve keys. Four are shown here; NewJazz says seven are possible. (NJ 2019-12 · 10:09)

Also taught as the rootless Mixolydian 13: keep the 3rd, ♭7, 9th and 13th, and drop the root (the bass has it), the 5th and the 11th (it clashes with the 3rd) — the same four notes as 2b a major third above the bass, E A B♭ D over C. (NJ 2018-02b · 06:20)

Grip 3: the tonic major, from two places

Grip 3 is a minor pentatonic scale, and it voices tonic major chords. There are two placements that work — which is why, running it round the cycle, every second chord uses the same notes in the left hand. (NJ 2018-07a · 02:05)

Bass a M6 below · 6/9

A minor pentatonic over C = 13 1 9 3 5 — C6/9. No 7th anywhere, so nothing is left wanting to move.

Bass a M3 below · ∆13

E minor pentatonic over C = 3 5 13 7 9 — C∆13. Same grip, brighter, with the major 7th in it.

The core progression: 1a → 2a → 1b → 2b

Descending fifths, alternating the grips and their inversions so the hand barely moves. Then change only the bass notes and the identical grip sequence becomes three different progressions. (NJ 2018-06 · 08:28)

A minor 7 → 7 bass: m3 below · m7 below B sus → 7 bass: m7 below · m7 below (Grip 1's bass dropped a fifth) C mi7 → 7alt → sus → 7 bass: m3 · M3 · m7 · m7 below

Same grips, same transitions, same fingering. Only the left-hand bass note is rewritten, and the progression changes character completely. This is the central claim of the system and it holds up under inspection.

Grips 4a, 4b and 5: dominants round the circle of fifths

Not NewJazz’s material — the extension grips from the grip table, used together. Grip 4a is 3 · 6 · 9 over a dominant, with 1 · ♭7 in the left hand. Grip 4b is 2 · 3 · 6 — grip 2a without its bottom note, so the chain below uses 2a. Grip 5 is 1 · ♭3 · 5 · ♭7 — a minor-7th shape — from the 3rd of a major chord: G B♭ D F over E♭ is E♭∆9. (user description) Grip 4a’s voicing is the V7 of the Mountain warmup — in C, left hand G F, right hand B E A (OS note opstIG1). Kellman voices a dominant the same way, 1 ♭7 | 3 13 9 (NK 2022-12-18 · 03:29–04:42), and uses the same three notes over a major chord: E A D over C, C6/9 (NK 2020-09-03 · 01:35).

ii–V–i in minor: Grip 2 alone

The whole minor cadence from one grip. In G minor, the sequence is 2a → 2a → 2b; inverted it becomes 2b → 2b → 2a, which lets you place it anywhere on the register. (NJ 2018-08 · 03:12)

iiø Am7♭5 sus4 grip 2a on E♭ bass ♭5 below E♭ G A D V D7 altered grip 2a on G♭ bass M3 below G♭ B♭ C F i Gm6/9 grip 2b on E bass M6 below E A B♭ D

The written chord symbols understate what you're playing — the grip expands every one of them. It isn't a iiø7, it's a iiø7 sus4; the tonic isn't a minor triad, it's a minor 6/9.

Also taught as three left-hand voicings that change a note or two: Dø9 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 9 → G7♯9♯5 ♭7 ♯9 3 ♯5 → Cm6/9 ♭3 5 6 9. The V and the i are the grip's own notes (2b a m7 above, 2a a m3 above); the ii keeps its ♭3 and 9 where the grip has the 1 and 11. (NK 2022-04-15 · 10:50–13:13; NK 2021-10-09 · 03:11–03:54)

One grip, three roots

The consequence of a rootless system, stated plainly. E♭ G A D is Grip 2a — and because B7alt and F13 turn out to be the same grip, the tritone substitution shows up here as a fact about the keyboard rather than a rule to memorize. (NJ 2018-05b · 33:57)

E♭ G A D over A = Am7♭5 (bass ♭5 below) E♭ G A D over B = B7alt (bass M3 below) E♭ G A D over F = F13 (bass m7 below)

Also taught as a scale fact: 7alt and 13♯11 a tritone apart share one melodic minor (B7alt = F13♯11 = C melodic minor). Over the A the grip's D is a suspended 4th; it can resolve down to the minor 3rd, C, or stay unresolved.

One grip, four chords, one scale

This is the shortcut the whole system is built toward. Take Grip 2a — say E♭ G A D — put it in the left hand and leave it there. Move only the bass, and the same four notes voice four different chords. Then add one right-hand grip in two positions, and you have the complete scale for every one of them. (NJ 2018-05b · 32:55)

Bass sits on the grip's…ChordGrip over that bassScale

major 3rdV7alt  B7alt3 · ♭13 · ♭7 · ♯9B altered
♭7V13♯11  F13♯11♭7 · 9 · 3 · 13F Lydian dominant
♭3i m(∆7)  Cm♭3 · 5 · 13 · 9C melodic minor

All four scales are modes of C melodic minor. The grip never moves; the bass chooses which mode you are hearing. That is the same bass-decides-everything principle as the rest of the system, now carrying four chords at once.

The right hand: 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8, twice

One five-finger grip — root, 4th, 5th, 6th, octave. Place it a half step below where the left-hand pinky sits, then place it again a whole step below that. Two positions, same fingering, and between them you can solo over all four chords without moving the left hand.

NewJazz states the rule differently, with the same result: play the triad whose root is under the left-hand middle finger, plus one a whole step below; use the left-hand thumb when the grip is inverted. (NJ 2020-11 · 03:07; NJ 2021-01 · 14:06) The pinky rule above is this page's way of saying it. Move the grip instead of the bass and the same two hands cover every melodic-minor mode: see Locomotive and wagon.

Also taught with ♭7 in place of the 6 — C F G B♭ C — as a rolling sixteenth-note ostinato that frees the left hand to change the harmony. (NK 2021-04-01 · 02:23–06:31)

The grip

E♭ G A D. Pinky on E♭ — that note is the reference for everything the right hand does.

Position 1

A half step below E♭ is D. From there: D G A B D.

Position 2

A whole step below that is C. From there: C F G A C.

Position 1 D G A B Position 2 C F G A Together they give C D F G A B — six notes. The grip adds the seventh: E♭. Total = C melodic minor, and nothing is left over.

The two hands are exact complements. The right hand can't produce the ♭3 and the left hand is already holding it, which is why the shape sounds complete rather than like a fragment.

The four chords, played

iiø7 · bass on the tritone

A underneath. Grip gives ♭5 ♭7 1 11; position 1 above stays within A Locrian ♮2; position 2 supplies the missing C and F.

V7alt · bass on the M3

B underneath, same grip, same right hand. Now it reads 3 ♭13 ♭7 ♯9 and the scale is B altered.

V13♯11 · bass on the ♭7

F underneath. The ♯11 isn't in the grip — it's the B in the right hand, which is exactly why the chord earns the name.

i minor · bass on the ♭3

C underneath. The grip alone is a m6/9; the B in the right hand is the major 7th that makes it a minor-major tonic.

The natural descent

Put the grip to work on a minor cadence and it produces a line that only ever moves downward. All three chords take grip 2a; the right hand enters one scale degree lower on each new chord, and drops one degree again within it. In C minor:

Entry degrees across the cadence: 4 · ♭3 → ♭3 · ♭2 → 2 · 1 Each chord begins where the previous one ended — one scale step lower — and the thumb drops a whole step again inside the chord.

This page's synthesis of two NewJazz lessons (grip 2a across the minor ii–V–i, 2018-08; triad pairs a whole step apart, 2018-09) — the descending thumb is not presented as such in the videos. Nothing new to memorize: the thumb is still a half step below the left-hand pinky, then a whole step below that. Because the three grips climb in minor thirds — A♭, B, E♭ — that fixed rule produces the descending entry degrees automatically. The left hand goes up; the right hand goes down.

And each pair completes its chord's scale exactly: the two thumbs plus the grip give D Locrian ♮2, then G altered, then C melodic minor — seven notes each, nothing spare. Steppable in the exercise player as NewJazz · the natural descent.

Simpler still: on every chord the two right-hand positions are the 1st and 2nd degree of the parent melodic minor, and the grip sits on its ♭3. The parent walks F → A♭ → C. That one sentence covers the whole cadence.

Also taught with a quartal shape: Cø as F♯ C F D (♭5 1 11 9), moved up a minor third over F for F7alt (A E♭ A♭ C♯ F). (NK 2023-01-24 · 05:18–06:07)

ii · Dm7♭5

Grip on A♭, thumb on G. Both hands together spell D Locrian ♮2 — all seven notes, nothing spare.

V · G7alt

Grip on B, thumb on B♭. Together: the complete G altered scale.

i · Cm∆7

Grip on E♭, thumb on D. Together: C melodic minor — and the B in the right hand is the major 7th that makes it a m∆7 rather than a m6/9.

Worked out in C minor

Same procedure, different key. For a Cm7♭5 the left-hand pinky goes on the tritone of C — G♭ — and the two right-hand positions follow from there automatically. This page's synthesis of two NewJazz lessons (grip 2a over the m7♭5, 2018-08; the right-hand placement rule, 2020-11).

Cm7♭5 LH pinky on G♭ (the tritone) grip: G♭ B♭ C F half step below G♭ → F position 1: F B♭ C D F whole step below F → E♭ position 2: E♭ A♭ B♭ C E♭ total: C D E♭ F G♭ A♭ B♭ = C Locrian ♮2 (6th mode of E♭ melodic minor)

You never work out the scale. You find the tritone, drop a half step, drop a whole step, and the fingering is identical in all twelve keys — which is the entire argument for hand grips over theory. The exercise player has this as Prehn · grip + row, steppable and transposable.

Grip simulator

Type any progression — up to sixteen chords, in standard or NewJazz spelling (Dmi7, CMa7, CmiMa7) — and the left-hand grips generate underneath, with Play the progression to hear them in time, one card per chord. It picks between the a and b inversions to keep the hand still — so the voicings it gives you are already voice-led, and the movement count tells you how far the hand travelled.

It reads m7, m7♭5, m6 and m∆7, plain and altered dominants, sus, and major tonics written as ∆7, 6 or 6/9. A dominant carrying any alteration — ♭9, ♯9, ♯5, ♭13 — is treated as altered and gets grip 2 in its altered placement. The simulator retains the grip and adds a defining tone when required: ♭3 for ø7, 7 for minor-major, and any explicitly requested altered extension. Major-7 symbols use the major-7 placement; 6/9 symbols use the sixth placement. Slash basses are preserved. Degree labels describe the actual played notes relative to the chord root.

The triad pairs, remembered as two minor chords

Every chord in a minor ii–V–i takes two major triads a whole step apart. Rather than memorizing three separate degree pairs, there's a shortcut: the roots of the upper triads spell the tonic minor triad, and the roots of the lower triads spell the minor triad a whole step below it. (NJ 2018-09 · 00:00; NJ 2018-05b · 09:45)

ChordLower triadUpper triadDegreesScale it spells

D7altA♭ — ♭3 of FmB♭ — ♭3 of Gm♭5 & ♭6D altered tones; add F♯ (3)
Gm6/9C — 5th of FmD — 5th of Gm4 & 5G melodic-minor tones; add B♭ (♭3)
In G minor you are playing the major triads built on the notes of Gm and of Fm — roots on the ii, thirds on the V, fifths on the i. Two minor triads, walked up in parallel, and the whole cadence is covered.
upper source Gm = G B♭ D lower source Fm = F A♭ C ii V i Am7♭5 D7alt Gm6/9 F & G A♭ & B♭ C & D roots thirds fifths

It transposes without rework. In C minor the two sources are Cm and B♭m: B♭ & C over the Dm7♭5, D♭ & E♭ over the G7alt, F & G over the Cm — the same ♭6/♭7, ♭5/♭6, 4/5 degrees, arrived at without counting any of them.

The lesson sheet numbers all three pairs from the key's tonic, G: ♭VII and I on the iiø (F, G), ♭II and ♭III on the V7alt (A♭, B♭), IV and V on the tonic (C, D). Counted from each chord's own root instead, the same pairs are ♭6 & ♭7, ♭5 & ♭6, and 4 & 5 — the labels used in the quick reference. Both are right. (NJ note NEWJAZZ7)

Also taught as Open Studio’s altered set: 3 and ♭7 in the left hand (F♯ C), with the A♭ or the B♭ triad on top, over D7alt. (OS workbook p.9)

On a m7, ♭3 & 4 — B♭ & C over Gm — spell Dorian rather than melodic minor. Kellman teaches it: E♭ + F over Cm7 gives C Dorian, and the same pair over F gives an F sus sound (NK 2022-02-20 · 03:48–04:28). The NewJazz lesson note lists it (NJ note NEWJAZZ7); the NewJazz video itself plays IV & V (C & D) over Gm6/9 (NJ 2018-05b · 28:14).

Also taught outside the minor cadence: C + D over C (C Lydian), E♭ + F over Cm7, E♭ + F minor over E♭ (gospel), and a minor triad with the major triad a whole step below for m11 — as inversions, four-note cells with a glue note, and wide arpeggios. (NK 2022-02-13 · 03:38–09:00; NK 2022-02-20 · 01:57–04:28; NK clip m11 arpeggo2 · 00:07–00:20)

Also taught over the V with a darker upper structure: D♭ over G is the shared triad, and A♭m9/G adds an F♯ — a major 7th over G, a ∆7♯5-type sound the triad pairs don't make (compare the Screendoor V in James Santangelo). (NK 2021-10-17 · 06:40–09:13)

Locomotive and wagon: every melodic-minor mode over one bass

The triad pairs, driven by the left hand. Grip 2a is the locomotive; the right hand hitches two major triads to it — the triad on the note under the left-hand middle finger, and the triad a whole step below. Keep the bass on C and move only the grip: point the middle finger at each note of C Aeolian major (C D E F G A♭ B♭) and the two hands cover all seven melodic-minor modes over that one bass. (NJ 2020-11 · 01:04; NJ 2021-01 · 03:20)

Grip 2a from an octave: lower the thumb a half step, index a tritone above the pinky, middle finger a whole step below the index → E♭ G A D (M3 · M2 · P4) Middle finger on G → G triad + F triad together C D E♭ F G A B = C melodic minor Middle finger on F → F triad + E♭ triad together C D♭ E♭ F G A B♭ = C Dorian ♭2 Middle finger on C, D, E, A♭, B♭ → the other five: Lydian augmented, Lydian dominant, Aeolian major, half-diminished, altered Check: the bass note must sit inside at least one of the grips.

With the grip on E♭ this is The right hand: 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8, twice — there the bass moves under a fixed grip; here the grip moves over a fixed bass. Invert the left hand (two lower notes up an octave) and hitch the triad to its thumb instead; place the grip anywhere, off the Aeolian-major notes, and the repeated pattern still holds the sound together as an outside colour.

Also taught as two licks on the same hands: left hand E♭ G A D over C, the right-hand triad grip run downward and stopped on one note (lick 1), or run upward to a smashing octave (lick 2), then moved over the fixed C bass through all seven modes; the right-hand middle finger can be added between index and ring. (NJ 2019-11 · 01:05)

The cycle, chord by chord

Seven chords round the cycle of fifths — a major ii–V–I landing on G, then a minor ii–V–i landing on E. All three grips appear, and the left hand barely leaves one position.

The right hand through the cycle: one grip, moving thumb

The same 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 grip covers every chord in the progression. You never change the fingering — you only change where the thumb lands. Each chord has two or three thumb positions — the triads NewJazz gives for that chord quality — and those positions plus the left-hand grip spell the chord's scale exactly, with nothing left over. (NJ 2020-02 · 04:11)

The pentatonic hand grip and the row

The right-hand half of the method. Place the hand on a minor pentatonic — thumb on the keynote, fingers stepwise up — and the grip is identical in every key. Then stack three of them. (NJ 2017-11 · 02:13)

The grip

1 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 · ♭7

Five fingers, five notes, same fingering in all twelve keys — which is the entire point. Once the hand knows it, you stop choosing notes and start making phrases.

The row

pos 1 → pos 2 → pos 3, a 5th apart

From F: F · C · G minor pentatonic. Left hand stays on position 1; the right hand moves freely between all three. Same grip, three places.

Thin it to a quartal

Lift fingers 4 and 2 and what's left is F B♭ E♭ — stacked fourths. The left hand's chord is already inside the scale shape.

The three positions together contain seven notes, not fifteen: F minor pentatonic F A♭ B♭ C E♭ C minor pentatonic C E♭ F G B♭ G minor pentatonic G B♭ C D F union = C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ = one diatonic collection (E♭ major) Over F that is 1 9 ♭3 11 5 13 ♭7 — F Dorian. Move the bass and you get the other modes.

So the row is a way of playing a whole seven-note scale while your hand only ever knows one five-note grip — and the same bass-note logic from the grips applies again: the collection is fixed, the bass decides which mode you're hearing.

Keep the bass on C and slide the three positions instead. Each step a fifth up brings in one sharpened note: E♭ · B♭ · F C Locrian B♭ · F · C C Phrygian ♭5 → 5 F · C · G C Aeolian ♭2 → 2 C · G · D C Dorian ♭6 → 6 G · D · A C Mixolydian ♭3 → 3 D · A · E C Ionian ♭7 → 7 A · E · B C Lydian 4 → ♯4 E · B · F♯ past Lydian the root itself sharpens, C → C♯ Up the row in fifths, brighter; up in fourths, darker. Blend positions and you blend modes.

Also taught as a left-hand comping voicing: F B♭ E♭ under an F blues, moved up F Mixolydian, and shifted to G♭ with the right hand. (NK 2022-09-11 · 01:48–04:36)

Also taught as multi-mode playing: the modes learned by sound from dark to bright, Locrian to Lydian, each one note away from its neighbour, then mixed by adding positions above or below. (NJ 2019-05 · 10:43–27:41; NJ 2021-03 · 03:12–04:21)

Also taught with a five-note step grip, 1 2 ♭3 4 5: E F♯ G A B and, a fourth up, A B C D E together spell C Lydian; each further fourth flattens one note — C major, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Moving to B♭ reuses most of the same positions; only two are new. (NJ 2022-07 · 02:06–09:00; NJ 2019-05 · 29:48)

Also taught as call and response between minor and major. Thumb on C and G: C natural minor without its ♭6. Thumb on A and E: C major without its 4th — and the ring finger can drop a half step to the tritone for a blue note. Alternate the two pairs as question and answer. (NJ 2021-03 · 05:26–08:56)

Also taught as the Dorian groundwork the row grew from. The three positions are one of three ways to build Dorian — as the 2nd mode of a major scale, as the major scale a whole step below played over the root, or as natural minor with its 6th raised — and neighbouring positions share two notes, the pivots for changing hand position (C and E♭ between F and C). Dorian sounds consonant because its minor-13 chord is a chain of perfect fifths with no tritone. And on a fixed D bass the same chain, started elsewhere, gives the other church modes: D for Dorian, A for Mixolydian, E for Ionian, G for Aeolian, C for Phrygian, F for Locrian. (NJ 2015-02 · 01:37–09:28; NJ 2016-12 · 00:00–03:08; NJ 2017-01 · 02:24; NJ 2017-09 · 01:42–02:39; NJ 2017-05 · 14:50–19:46; NJ 2017-07 · 12:21)

More grips that fill a mode: Modal playgrounds.

Modal playgrounds

Triad add-2: seven modes over one bass

A major triad with its 5th doubled and the 2 added — thumb and pinky an octave apart on the 5th, ring finger on the 3rd. From the thumb that is the 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 grip. Put the index finger on C, F and G — a 1-4-5 relation — and the three positions spell the C major collection: C major over C, D Dorian over D, and so on up the bass. Hold the bass on C instead and move the three positions. (NJ 2024-07-31 · 01:06)

The Lydian playground: a recipe

The add-2 grip from the block above, placed on the triads of I, V and II — C, G and D — fills C Lydian. The lesson is less about the scale than about how to build a place to play in, step by step. (NJ 2023-04 · 01:04)

1 Pick a mode C Lydian 2 Pick a grip that fills it triad + 2 on C, G, D (B Lydian: B, F♯, C♯) 3 Make a progression C Lydian → B Lydian → Lydian on each white key, stepping down 4 Left hand root, 5th, octave, maybe the 2nd on top — drop the 2nd low down 5 Move the hands contrary or oblique motion 6 Make motifs a 1-2-4 arpeggio · the grip's top minor 3rd on fingers 4-5 as call and answer · fingers 1 and 5 together · 3-2 to close 7 Build one main phrase, vary it, play around

The D position carries the F♯, so it is the one that makes the sound Lydian; the C and G positions alone are plain C major.

The fifth-fifth grip: a Dorian playground

A symmetric grip: an octave with two notes inside, thumb to middle finger a perfect 5th and index to pinky a perfect 5th — 1 · 4 · 5 · 8. Dorian is symmetric too, so the grip fits it from five places. (NJ 2019-10 · 02:02)

The thumb notes G B♭ C D F are G minor pentatonic — the minor pentatonic on the 5th of the Dorian key. A Dorian → thumb on E minor pentatonic. The other seven thumb notes each put a note outside the mode. Left hand: the C bass, or the same grip on the same positions — thinned to fewer notes low down. Block chords or arpeggios, in several octaves.

Also taught as an ostinato: C F G C in either hand, for hand independence rather than as a Dorian playground — see Ostinatos in Warmups. (NK 2021-03-25 · 02:25–09:46; NK 2021-04-01 · 03:35–05:13)

The Locrian golden trick

Over C Dorian the minor-pentatonic grip sits on C, G and D — the row from the key note. To jazz it up, jump a minor 3rd to E♭ and run the row from there: E♭, B♭, F spell C Locrian. Play mostly Dorian and visit Locrian now and then; keep running the Locrian row upward and it leads straight back into the Dorian row. (NJ 2023-11a · 09:35; NJ 2024-09-30 · 01:24)

The mega chord: the row as one chord

Leave the middle finger out of the minor-pentatonic grip and a minor-7 arpeggio is left. Stack those up the row — C, G, D — and the thirds alternate minor and major with only perfect fifths inside: C E♭ G B♭ D F A, a Dorian minor 13. Keep alternating past the octave instead of repeating Dorian and each new grip adds a note from outside, until all twelve are in. (NJ 2023-07 · 01:05)

The several-octave mode

One five-note grip, 1 · 2 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 (C D E♭ F G), placed a 4th higher each time over a C bass. Each new position lowers one note, so the mode darkens as the hand climbs: Aeolian low down, Phrygian above it, Locrian at the top. (NJ 2018-02a · 02:17)

Dorian over a bass a half step up

Play Dorian with the plain row and move the bass a half step above its key note: D Dorian over E♭, E♭ Dorian over E. The bass is foreign to the mode, yet the mode holds. (NJ 2016-06 · 01:33–10:46)

The chord itself from the 7th: G and B are its 3rd and ♯5, D its major 7th, doubled.

Grip 2 · E♭ A♭ C E♭

The same grip a half step up — root, 11 and 13, the colour above the chord.

Grip 3 · C D E♭

A stepwise three-finger grip: whole step, then half step. NewJazz gives no direction — play it either way.

Grip 4 · F G A♭

The same three-finger grip a fourth higher — it is the only grip with the F.

Two ways to see grips 1 and 2

As a hand shape · 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 without the 5 (this page's reading)

The familiar 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 right-hand shape from D and from E♭, with the 5th (marked) left out. Dropping it is what keeps the grip inside harmonic minor: A and B♭ aren't in C harmonic minor. Same fingering for both, a half step apart.

As triads · how NewJazz teaches it

Two major triads in second inversion, the pinky doubling the 5th on top: G major as D G B + D, and A♭ major as E♭ A♭ C + E♭.

The rule: every harmonic-minor mode holds two major triads a half step apart, sitting just below the augmented 2nd. In C harmonic minor that gap is A♭–B, and the triads are G and A♭ — the V and ♭VI.

Source: NewJazz video (Evernote note NEWJAZZ9), E♭∆7♯5 lesson; the only fingering given is "pinky hits the fifth" — the 5th of each triad.

grips 1 + 2 D E♭ G A♭ B C harmonic-minor hexatonic C D E♭ G A♭ B (no 4th) grips 3 + 4 C D E♭ · F G A♭ minor hexatonic C D E♭ F G A♭ (no 7th) all four C harmonic minor C D E♭ F G A♭ B

Also taught as one of the seven harmonic-minor modes, each a church mode with one note sharpened — each one, as a chord with its tensions, is in The Chord Atlas under Harmonic Minor (NewJazz: Locrian ♯6 for Locrian ♮6, Mixolydian ♯1 for Mixolydian ♭♭7). The triad-pair rule holds in every mode and key: F Ionian ♯5 has B♭ and A, C Phrygian dominant has D♭ and C — each pair sits just below that mode's augmented 2nd.

Also taught as a voicing: E (2nd inv.) + E♭ (2nd inv.) over E — E Lydian ♯2, the 6th mode of G♯ harmonic minor; E and E♭ are its V and ♭VI triads. (NK 2020-08-06 · 03:38–05:26)

This page's extension, not a NewJazz lesson — the video uses the grips only over E♭∆7♯5. Why it travels: E♭∆7♯5 is a rootless Cm∆9, so the same four grips sit over the tonic of a minor key — and C harmonic minor also covers that key's Dm7♭5 (Locrian ♮6) and G7♭9♭13 (Phrygian dominant). Over the G7 the grips read 5 1 3 5, ♭13 ♭9 11, ♭13 5 11 and ♭9 1 ♭7. The cadence is set up as the Harmonic minor · NewJazz tab in the ii–V–I Lab, and the hexatonic appears under every chord it fits in What plays over what.

Major ii–V–I with the row

The same minor-pentatonic grip from the row, now over Dm7 | G7 | C∆7. Start the row on the ii's root — D · A · E — and the three grips are all white keys: D Dorian over the Dm7, G Mixolydian over the G7, C major over the C∆7. Then two more rows add colour, each on one chord only. (NJ 2017-12 · 04:43)

The pentatonic row is also listed as right-hand grips in the Classical and Lydian I tabs of the ii–V–I Lab. Stacking the arpeggios without the middle finger further up the row is the mega chord.

The simplest path keeps one parent for all three chords: C harmonic minor D Locrian ♮6 → G Phrygian dominant → C harmonic minor C harmonic major D Dorian ♭5 → G Mixolydian ♭2 → (resolves to C major, not minor) The two differ by one note — E♭ or E. That note is the ♭13 or 13 of the V.

Names vary between teachers. "Half-diminished scale" usually means Locrian ♮2 — NewJazz and Kellman both call it Locrian ♯2, naming each alteration against the plain mode, and "Super Locrian" is the altered scale — normally a V7alt choice; over Dm7♭5 it fits because its ♭3 and ♭5 are the chord's. The same menu is in the Minor ii–V–i tab of the ii–V–I Lab and under each chord in What plays over what. (NK 2023-01-24 · 02:03; NK 2021-03-04 · 12:48)

Also taught entirely from melodic-minor modes: D Locrian ♮2 (half-diminished; NewJazz and Kellman: Locrian ♯2) → G altered over G7alt → C melodic minor. Kellman runs the same path as one continuous line, stepping to the nearest note at each change. (NJ 2018-01 · 08:27–12:45; NK 2021-10-09 · 04:24–07:15)

Also taught as a chart. NewJazz files every seven-note scale into four families of seven — major modes, melodic-minor modes, harmonic-minor modes, harmonic-major modes: the Parent column in both menus — and names each one as a church mode with one note changed: melodic minor = Dorian ♯7, Dorian ♭2 = Phrygian ♯6, Lydian augmented = Lydian ♯5, Lydian dominant = Mixolydian ♯4, Aeolian dominant = Aeolian ♯3, the altered scale = Ionian ♯1; harmonic minor = Aeolian ♯7, Phrygian dominant = Phrygian ♯3; harmonic major = Ionian ♭6. Add the symmetric scales — two diminished, one whole tone, two augmented — and the count is 33, the Symmetric row above. (NJ 2023-05 · 03:01–18:21; NJ 2019-09 · 01:24–12:08)

NewJazz blues — the lessons in order

Everything from here down is the blues half of the method: hand shapes rather than scales. Learn it in this order — each step only adds to the one before.

Lesson 2 is all G blues over a G7 — the video says "the blues in G" and names no chord; G7 and the grouping below come from your own description of the lesson images. Tricks 1 and 3 can be used on their own; Trick 2 is taught as one sequence.

Lesson 1 · the fingering: the three-finger engine

The blues reduced to one hand position and three fingers. Thumb, index and middle sit on 1 · ♭3 · 4; then the same three fingers move up and sit on 4 · ♭5 · 5. That's the entire mechanism — everything else is added on top of it. (NJ 2021-12b · 01:07–02:23)

Grip A · 1 ♭3 4

G B♭ C

Fingers 1, 2, 3. The ♭3 is the blue third; the 4 is where you lean.

Grip B · 4 ♭5 5 (the three-finger chromatic grip, NJ 2021-09)

C D♭ D

The same three fingers, shifted. Three adjacent semitones containing the ♭5 — this is where the grit lives.

End to end

G B♭ C D♭ D — five of the six minor-blues notes. The sixth, the ♭7, comes from the engine's second position, on D: D F G — same three fingers. NewJazz also shows a G B♭ B variant, minor 3rd to major 3rd.

The two grips share the 4, so the hand pivots on one note rather than jumping. Learn the engine before adding anything: the whole method is three fingers first, then fingers 4 and 5 as decoration, then jazz vocabulary on top.

Lesson 1 · zapping: inside, outside, minor and major

Because the engine's grips keep their fingering in every key, moving them is a way to colour the blues without new technique. Shift the whole G-blues engine up a half step and it becomes A♭ blues — outside the G tonality — then come home. Over a C vamp the same grips give C minor blues or C major blues; zap between the two for the minor–major rub, and out to E♭ minor blues for tension. The videos name no chord — a modal G blues over a bass on the key, 4th and 5th, and a C blues over a four-beat bass that suggests major. The minor–major rub implies a dominant 7, so read the vamps as G7 and C7 (this page's reading). (NJ 2021-09 · 08:14; NJ 2021-10 · 02:16)

Same fingering in every key, even when the thumb lands on black keys — get used to it rather than re-fingering. Grip positions follow the engine rule (Grip A on the 1 and the 5, Grip B on the 4); the lessons show them on the keys rather than naming each one. In the altered rows the blue note is the 13 (E over G7, A over C7).

Over a minor chord instead, the minor-third-up grip is the golden trick: the row a minor third up gives the Locrian colour — see The Locrian golden trick in Modal playgrounds.

Also taught with the dominant pentatonic, side-slipping on the IV of the blues — see Dominant Pentatonic in Pentatonics; the left-hand fourths follow. (NK 2021-02-12 · 11:14–12:10)

Lesson 1 · blues grips through a ii–V–I

Over ‖: Dm7 | G7 | C∆7 | C∆7 :‖ — rather than changing scale at every bar, you move between blues grips, and several of them carry across the chord change unaltered. Fingering for every grip in this lesson is the engine above: thumb, index and middle on 1 · ♭3 · 4, then the same three fingers on 4 · ♭5 · 5, counted from the grip's own root. (NJ 2022-01 · 02:21)
