Hover or tap a grip to light every row with the same six notes — the same hand shape, renamed by the chord underneath.

The relative pairs. A major blues grip and the minor blues grip a minor third below are the same six notes — only the home note differs. C major blues = A minor blues C D E♭ E G A G major blues = E minor blues G A B♭ B D E F major blues = D minor blues F G A♭ A C D

That equivalence is what makes the lesson work. The three grips over the Dm7 sit a fifth apart — D, A, E — and two of them are already the grips you want on the G7, relabelled. You don't change hand position at the bar line; you change which note you treat as home.

The bracket on the ii. The three grips together are D Dorian plus three blue notes: D minor blues D F G A♭ A C A minor blues A C D E♭ E G E minor blues E G A B♭ B D together C D E F G A B + A♭ E♭ B♭ (the ♭5 of D, A and E)

Why D · A · E here, but D · A · F · C pentatonics in the bucket? Different key, different job. The bucket vamp is in D minor (one flat — its step grips carry B♭) and goes nowhere, so it mixes two inside grips with two deliberately outside ones (F, C) to step out and back. This ii–V–I is in C, so the ii is D Dorian with B natural — the E minor blues supplies it — and the grips have to lead somewhere. Going the sharp way round the fifths, D → A → E, lands on A minor blues = C major blues and E minor blues = G major blues: the grips for the V and the I. The bucket's circle runs F · C · G · D · A toward the flats for colour; this one runs D · A · E toward the sharps for connection. The plain row is in The pentatonic hand grip and the row.

On the ii

D minor blues over Dm7 — 1 ♭3 4 ♭5 5 ♭7, with A♭ the blue note against D Dorian.

The pivot grip

A C D E♭ E G. Call it A minor blues on the Dm7 and C major blues on the G7 — identical notes, no hand movement.

On the V

G major blues over G7 — 1 9 ♭3 3 5 13. The B♭ rubbing against the B is the whole point of a blues dominant.

Also taught with chromatic notes, over a ii–V–I in F: the engine's three fingers move freely through all twelve notes under two rules — the index finger always lands on a black key, and no finger plays twice in a row. The F major blues scale on the engine is home base to come back to (the same notes as D minor blues, by the relative pairs above). Then arpeggiate each chord with all five fingers and mix in chromatic and blues notes. The bass walks root, 5th and a leading note into the next chord. (NJ 2021-12a · 02:18–12:16)

Lesson 2 · Trick 1: the pinky — on the 6th or the octave

Once the three-finger engine is secure, the pinky extends it. It has two homes: the octave or the 6th — so over a G blues, G or E. Nothing else changes. (NJ 2021-12b · 03:24)

The octave closes the grip and sounds settled; the 6th opens it and is where the blues starts sounding like jazz, since the 6 is the one note that pulls the line toward a major-blues colour.

A third option in the same lesson: the ring finger on D, the 5th, above the G B♭ C grip — leave out the middle finger if the stretch is awkward.

Lesson 2 · Trick 2: the climb — 1 ♭3 4 8, four positions as one sequence

Thumb, index, middle and pinky on 1 · ♭3 · 4 · 8. Then move the whole grip: G → A → B♭ → B, a whole step and then two half steps. Treat it as one gesture, not four options — that grouping is from your description of the lesson images; in the video he simply moves the grip and pinky up a whole step and two half steps. (NJ 2021-12b · 05:32)

Ascending G B♭ C G → A C D A → B♭ D♭ E♭ B♭ → B D E B Descending the same four, reversed — start from the B Over a G7 the four positions read: G 1 ♭3 4 home A 9 4 5 still inside B♭ ♭3 ♭5 ♭13 outside B 3 5 13 resolves onto the major 3rd

Home · from G

The minor-pentatonic position. Establishes where the blues is before you leave it.

Still inside · from A

9 4 5. A whole step up and still inside the G sound — the step before the climb leaves home.

Out · from B♭

♭3 ♭5 ♭13 — the furthest from home, and the reason the landing works.

In · from B

3 5 13. You arrive on the major third of the chord, which is why the whole climb sounds resolved rather than abandoned.

The four positions together cover nine of the twelve notes, omitting only the ♭9, the ♭7 and the 7 — so it reads as deeply chromatic while never contradicting the chord's own ♭7. Steppable in the exercise player as NewJazz · blues climb.

Lesson 2 · Trick 3: jazz extensions — the full minor pentatonic on the engine's three positions

Add fingers 4 and 5 to the three-finger engine at each of its three positions — D, G and E — and each becomes a full minor pentatonic, 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7. (NJ 2021-12b · 11:50–12:55)

D minor pentatonic D F G A C over G7: 5 ♭7 1 9 11 the 9 and 11 G minor pentatonic G B♭ C D F over G7: 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7 the home blues E minor pentatonic E G A B D over G7: 13 1 9 3 5 the 13 and 9 — E minor = G major pentatonic together G A B♭ B C D E F — G Mixolydian plus the blue ♭3

The E position is the relative-minor move from Lesson 1: E minor pentatonic has the same notes as G major pentatonic, so it brings in the bright side of the blues without a new grip. Nothing in the three clashes with the chord. Earlier versions of this page put the pentatonics on the four climb roots; the source puts them on the engine's positions.

Also in the blues lessons: the four-key chromatic grip — thumb on B

Four fingers on four adjacent keys, B C C♯ D. Over G7 that's 3 · 4 · ♯11 · 5 — a chromatic run from the major 3rd up to the 5th, filling the gap the minor-pentatonic grips skip over. In the lessons it follows the engine grips. The notes were read from the on-screen dots and confirmed by me. (NJ 2020-05 · 01:40)

The bucket · grips to reach for over a vamp

The improvising method in one picture: put a handful of grips in a bucket, set a bass vamp going, and reach in. You stop choosing notes and start choosing grips — and because each grip is one hand shape, the choice is physical rather than theoretical. (NJ 2020-07 · 02:02)

Minor-pentatonic grip

1 · ♭3 · 4 · 5 · ♭7

A minor pentatonic under five fingers. The workhorse — same fingering in every key.

Step grip

1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5

The first five notes of a major scale. Adjacent keys, no gaps — which is why it sounds smooth and singing rather than bluesy.

Blues grip

4 · ♭5 · 5 · 1

G A♭ A D — the ♭5 with a neighbour on each side, plus the root. A grip that exists purely to deliver the blue note.

A worked bucket: bass on D · F · G · A

A D-minor vamp in quarter notes — 1 ♭3 4 5 — with seven grips to reach for. Four sit entirely inside; three add colour. (user description)

GripNotesOver the D bass
D minor pentatonicD F G A C1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7inside
A minor pentatonicA C D E G5 ♭7 1 9 4inside
C stepC D E F G♭7 1 9 ♭3 4inside
F stepF G A B♭ C♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7inside
G bluesG A♭ A D4 ♭5 5 1the blue note
C minor pentatonicC E♭ F G B♭♭7 ♭9 ♭3 4 ♭6colour

Inside · D minor pentatonic

Everything lands. Use it to establish where home is before you leave it.

Outside · F minor pentatonic

The same grip a minor third up, and now four of the five notes are altered. Reach for it, then reach back.

The five grip roots are a chain of fifths: F → C → G → D → A D and A are the inside pentatonics F and C are the outside pentatonics G's slot holds the blues grip instead of a plain pentatonic Any three adjacent positions spell one mode — see the row; reaching past three is what takes you outside.

The minor-3rd jump to F and C is NewJazz's Locrian golden trick, here in D: see The Locrian golden trick.

Lesson 3 · tetrachords: 1 · ♭3 · 4 · ♭5 on the 3rd and the 6th

The soloing shortcut for a dominant blues. Take the first four notes of a minor blues scale — 1 ♭3 4 ♭5 — and place that one tetrachord twice: once on the 3rd of the chord, once on the 6th. Two hand positions, no scale to work out. (NJ 2019-03 · 01:00; NJ 2018-04 · 01:04)

On the 3rd

C7 → from E

E G A B♭ — which over C is 3 · 5 · 6 · ♭7. Every note a strong chord tone; this is the consonant half.

On the 6th

C7 → from A

A C D E♭ — over C that's 6 · 1 · 9 · ♭3. This is where the blue note comes from.

Both together

C D E♭ E G A B♭ — 1 2 ♭3 3 5 6 ♭7. The major blues scale with the ♭7 added, assembled from one grip placed twice.

Through a blues in C: C7 from E: E G A B♭ from A: A C D E♭ F7 from A: A C D E♭ from D: D F G A♭ G7 from B: B D E F from E: E G A B♭ Moving I7 → IV7 you keep one tetrachord (A C D E♭). Moving V7 → I7 you keep the other (E G A B♭).

That overlap is the practical payoff: across the whole twelve bars you are only ever moving one of your two hand positions at a time. One note to check: on the 3rd of C the tetrachord ends on B♭, not A♭ — ♭5 above E is B♭. The second tetrachord, A C D E♭, is exactly right as written.

The 2018-04 lesson finds the same two positions with the index finger as pointer — on the chord's root or its 5th — and adds the pinky a major 3rd above the top note (A C D E♭ G over C7), plus a slide from E♭ up to E (B♭ up to B from the 5th).

Also taught as a phrase sandbox over a C vamp: the same grip at its two positions, thumb on A and on E, with three motifs — step, jump and arch — moved between positions and octaves. (NJ 2019-02 · 05:21)

The six soloing devices

The companion list to the grips — what to actually play over them, in the order they're usually introduced. Each is a way of decorating chord tones rather than a new scale to learn. (NJ 2019-06 · 03:28; NJ 2019-07 · 02:05)

1 Arpeggios the chord tones themselves, in any order 2 Leading tones a half step below or above a chord tone, resolving to it 3 Chromatic tones passing notes filling the gaps between them 4 Blues the E minor blues scale over the whole cycle 5 Diminished structures symmetric shapes over dominants 6 Tritone substitutions playing the dominant a tritone away instead
Device 1 in practice — over the seven-chord cycle, Am7 D7 G∆7 C∆7 F♯m7♭5 B7 Em∆7: arpeggiate each chord root position → 1st → 2nd → 3rd inversion, and back connect the chords through the nearest inversion, alternating up and down then improvise: one inversion per chord, one or two notes at first, short phrases with breaks Left hand: a walking bass — root, 5th, root, then a leading tone a half step from the next root.

5 · diminished

D7 with a ♭9 and no root is four notes a minor 3rd apart, F♯ A C E♭ — and B7♭9 without its root is the same four. Move it up in minor 3rds.

6 · tritone sub

F7 over the B bass adds the ♭9 and ♭5. A♭7 over D does the same for the D7: D7♭9♭5.

Also taught as 51 licks in seven levels over the same cycle: arpeggio; plus chromatic notes; the E minor blues scale; arpeggio with blues; all three; the triad grip (the add-2 grip); everything mixed. Master one level before adding the next. (NJ 2020-03 · 01:05–17:33)

Also taught with scales instead of arpeggios: run each chord's scale and, at every change, step to the nearest note of the next scale — never restart from its root. (NK 2020-10-15 · 01:59–04:30; NK 2021-10-09 · 06:11–07:15)

Also taught as eight diminished licks: any cell — C D♭ G♭, E♭ E G C, a major triad — moved in minor thirds; see Up in minor thirds in Playing Out.

More on items 5 and 6 in Special Scales and the Substitution Finder; items 2 and 3 are the enclosures in the Blues.

Rhythm and coordination

Four exercises for time rather than notes. Two need no piano at all — tapping and the foot; the other two — five against four and odd motifs — put an odd-length pattern against an even pulse until the hands stop needing the bar line.

Tapping: fast and steady

Speed and evenness trained away from the keyboard, by tapping on a table, then moved onto a grip. (NJ 2020-09 · 05:32–17:25)

Rules tap slowly and steadily before speeding up stop at any tension until the hand is loose again lift one finger at a time to catch stray twitches — the ring finger is hardest Exercises fingers in a row · two fingers · 3-tap and 7-tap patterns against 16ths · free Both hands the left taps four to the bar while the right taps 16ths in a 3- or 7-tap pattern Then the same patterns on the minor-pentatonic grip, at different positions

Steadiness comes first: any note works if it is played in time.

The foot as the steady beat

The left foot keeps time — heel on beat 1, forefoot on beat 2, with the metronome — while everything above it is free. The right foot stays free for the pedal. (NJ 2023-01 · 03:18–24:38)

1 Foot on the beat, then look away · talk · talk nonsense · sing freely — the foot never moves off it 2 Swap the voice for fingers: one finger press for each free sound 3 Fast tempo: double the metronome but keep the foot slow; with a band, put the foot on half time 4 Expert: speed a pattern up and slow it down while the foot stays put 5 At the piano: minor-pentatonic grips in both hands, a Dorian row in the right

NewJazz calls the foot the "locomotive" here — a different image from Locomotive and wagon, where the locomotive is the left-hand grip.

Five against four: 5 · 4 · 2 · 1 · 3

The right hand plays the D minor-pentatonic grip in a five-note finger pattern, 5-4-2-1-3, one note per 16th. Five against four, so the pattern starts on a different 16th each time round. The left hand plays the same grip an octave lower, thinned to a quartal, every time the right-hand pinky plays. (NJ 2019-04 · 01:02–08:49)

Right hand D F G A C, fingers 1–5 → C A F D G, repeated, one per 16th Left hand the grip thinned to fingers 1, 3, 5: D G C — on every right-hand 5 Metronome 60 Then the row: D, A and E grips over the D left hand (D Dorian) · other odd patterns of 3, 5, 7, 9

The left-hand chord follows a finger, not a beat — so it lands on every 16th in turn. The quartal is the row's lift-two-fingers thinning.

Odd motifs against four sub-beats

A slow left-hand bass, one note per beat on fingers 1-5-4-3, with four sub-beats felt inside each beat. Against it the right hand builds a pentatonic grip one finger at a time, and each stage adds a motif whose length doesn't divide by four. (NJ 2021-02 · 01:29–36:58)

StageNotesEven motifOdd motif
2B♭ D♭1-2 · mirror 2-1— add breaks
3+ E♭1-2-3-21-2-3 · mirror 3-2-1
4+ F1-2-3-41-2-1-2-4-3-2
5+ A♭ — the full grip1-2-3-4-5-4-3-21-2-1-2-5-4-3

Metronome at 52. Learn each motif note by note without the metronome, then with it, then freely — about 30 minutes strict, 15 free. The left-hand bass notes aren't given in the lesson.

Stride & Ragtime

The left hand is the band.

Before the rhythm section existed, the left hand played it: bass note on the strong beats, chord on the weak ones, and a harmonic vocabulary built almost entirely from chromatic approach rather than modulation. Everything here is in G.

Ragtime almost never changes key inside a strain. What sounds like harmonic motion is a diminished or augmented chord passing between two diatonic ones — a half step of bass movement doing the work of a modulation.

The left hand

Bass and chord

1 & 3 bass · 2 & 4 chord

The engine. Single bass note low, three-note chord in the middle register, strictly alternating. Keep the chord quiet and the bass even — the swing comes from steadiness, not accent. (NK 2020-06-18 · 00:33–01:48)

The tenth

root + 3rd, ten notes apart

The stride bass proper. If you can't span it, roll it — bass note, then the 3rd a fraction later. Broken tenths are idiomatic, not a compromise. (NK 2020-06-18 · 01:57–02:47; NK 2020-06-25 · 01:10–01:25)

Walking the bass line

A → B → C → C♯

The last bar of the arrangement: Am7 – G/B – C6 – C♯°7. The chords exist to harmonize a bass line that is simply climbing by step. Inversions aren't decoration here, they're how the line stays smooth.

Three passing chords that do everything

♯IV°7 → I⁶₄

C → C♯°7 → G/D

The signature ragtime cadence, and it happens twice in your chart. Bass climbs C–C♯–D; the tonic lands in second inversion, so it reads as a breath rather than an ending. Everything about the idiom is in this one move.

♭VI°7 → V7

E♭°7 → D7

Bar 8. The diminished sits a half step above the dominant and falls into it — three of its four notes are already in D7, so only the bass really moves.

III7 and III7♯5

B7♯5 → B7 → C

Bar 2. The raised 5th of B7 is G — the note it came from — and it resolves up to the 3rd of the IV chord. An augmented dominant is a half-step machine with the answer already inside it.

Your arrangement, playable

The sixteen bars from the score, the same sixteen bars stripped bare, and the ♯IV°7 cadence on its own to loop. Click any chord to hear it; press play to run the strain.

The form

Ragtime is sectional, not cyclical — it borrows its shape from the march, not the song. Nobody solos; you play the strains.

Each strain is 16 bars, usually 4 + 4 + 4 + 4. Classic order: A A B B A C C D D The C strain — the "trio" — moves to the subdominant and usually stays there. Repeats are written, not optional: the B strain is heard twice before A returns.

The trio's key change is the only real modulation in the whole form, which is why it lands. Everything inside a strain — the diminished chords, the augmented dominants, the inversions — is chromatic motion within one key, and that distinction is the difference between playing ragtime and playing a jazz tune with old chords in it.

The right hand: octave chords

Melody in octaves, chord tones inside: a diatonic triad between the thumb and the pinky, walked through the chord's scale. Over Am: E A C E (5 1 ♭3 5), moved through A Dorian — only the F♯ is black. (NK 2020-06-18 · 05:56–07:56; NK 2021-12-04 · 09:54–12:31)

1 Octave melody alone, then fill the octave with the triad of the scale step 2 Keep the inner notes fixed while the octave moves; re-voice on bigger jumps 3 Art Tatum's version: a triad inside an octave moved up F Dorian, then change only the top and bottom notes 4 Erroll Garner's: on E♭ with G on top, G … E♭ … G inside; flick from black keys to white 5 On a ballad: diatonic triads with the top note doubled below

Octaves on black keys: thumb and 4, then 4 → 5 for a smooth move (NK 2020-08-27 · 05:55–08:36). Tatum (NK 2020-07-09 · 05:27–07:01); ballads (NK 2022-01-23 · 05:42–07:55). Another right-hand device: the thumb holds a note while fingers 3 and 5 rock a minor third in rhythm — over A♭6, then F7 → B♭7 (NK 2020-06-18 · 08:49–09:28). The same outer octave with a 6/°7 inside is the Shearing block.

Left-hand practice

How to build the stride left hand, collected from his stride lessons. (NK 2020-06-18 · 00:33–08:49; NK 2020-06-25 · 00:44–03:44; NK 2021-12-04 · 02:24–14:17)

The two pedal methods are both his, from different lessons; try both.

Erroll Garner: the bounce and the flick

A chord on all four beats in the left hand — simple, even, root-position voicings — and the right hand hanging back behind it. Practise on the changes of "Misty" in E♭: E♭∆ → B♭m7 → E♭7 → A♭∆. (NK 2020-08-27 · 01:42–04:31; NK 2020-08-27 · 09:11–10:25)

The flick pinky on the bass, then bounce up to the other two notes — E♭ as 1 3 7: E♭, then G D (read from his keys); also on the "and" of 4 Open B♭m B♭, then A♭ D♭ (♭7 ♭3) Closed E♭7 G D♭ Right hand a scale or simple melody over the bounce first, then improvise; then lay it back

Garner's ballad left hand — the voicing arpeggiated — is in The piano as an orchestra (Solo Piano); his octave chords are above.

Art Tatum: off-beats and the cycle

Two Tatum devices beyond the tenths and the runs: land the right hand on the "ands" rather than on 1 and 3 — practise with plain octaves on the off-beats — and reharmonize a ii–V–I as dominants round the cycle of fourths. (NK 2020-07-09 · 03:54–04:54; NK 2020-07-09 · 13:38–15:13)

Original Fm9 – B♭13 – E♭∆9 Reharm F7 B♭7 E♭7 A♭7 D♭7 G♭7, then the ii–V–I Double time further round: … G♭7 B7 E7 A7 D7 G7 C7 Fm7 B♭7 E♭

Also from this lesson: an alternating two-hand run — C–D♭ in the right hand (2–3), F–G♭ in the left (3–2), up and down the keyboard — and a parallel two-hand arpeggio over Dø / Fm6, the left hand 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7 (5 3 2 1), the right ♭7 1 ♭3 ♭5 (1 2 3 4) (NK 2020-07-09 · 10:30–13:31). His C dominant run is in Arpeggios.

Giant Steps as stride

A stride left hand through the Coltrane cycle, B∆ – D7 – G∆ – B♭7 – E♭∆. (NK 2022-03-20 · 01:59–16:11)

1 A bass note plus voice-led left-hand chords kept in one register — major 6 inversions, rootless 7 9 3 5 2 Then mix 5ths, 7ths and 10ths, rolled if needed: a 5th on B, 10ths on D and G, 1 3 ♭7 on B♭7, 1 5 then 2 5 on E♭ 3 Walking tenths up a scale into Dsus → D7 4 Passing seventh chords a half step above or below: Am – E♭7 – D7, or Am – D♭7 – D7 5 Right hand: the melody in octaves, then octave chords, then passing octave notes with finger 4 (Garner-like), then solo

The video is 360p, so nothing here is read from the keys.

Forms and changes

This page's own reference, not a lesson from the sources: the forms a stride player is expected to know, written in C.

32 bars, AABA A | C C♯°7 | Dm7 D♯°7 | C/E A7 | D7 G7 | | C C7 | F F♯°7 | C/G A7 | D7 G7 | A the same eight bars B | E7 | E7 | A7 | A7 | D7 | D7 | G7 | G7 | A the same eight bars, ending on C
ItemWhat to know
Rhythm changesthe other 32-bar form everyone knows — I Got Rhythm's changes: see Rhythm Changes
Multi-strain (shout) formHarlem stride pieces keep ragtime's layout — several 16-bar strains, each repeated, often a later strain in a new key — rather than a song's AABA; see The form above
The passing-diminished walk-upC C♯°7 Dm7 D♯°7 C/E — the bass climbs by half steps; each diminished chord is a rootless 7♭9 leading up to the next chord (see Secondary dominant and diminished)
The left-hand patternbass on 1 and 3, chord on 2 and 4 — Bass and chord, above

Solo-piano methods beyond stride are in Solo Piano.

Block Chords & Locked Hands

Harmonize the melody itself.

Every other technique here puts chords under a line. Block chords make the line into chords: every melody note gets its own voicing, both hands move in parallel, and the tune arrives as a slab of harmony. It's the sound of Shearing, Garland's choruses, and every big-band sax soli ever written.

A block-chord passage has no accompaniment and no solo. There is only the melody, thickened — which is why the rhythm of the melody becomes the rhythm of the whole texture.

Three ways to thicken a note

Drop 2

take the 2nd voice down an octave

Close-position C∆7 is C E G B. Drop the second voice from the top (G) an octave and you get G · C E B — the standard guitar and big-band spacing. There are four of these per chord; the full treatment is below.

Drop 3

take the 3rd voice down an octave

Drop the third voice instead (E) and the gap opens lower. Wider and darker than drop 2 — good for ballads and for the bottom of a big spread. (OS clip Sugar Chords · 03:55–04:25)

Shearing block

melody doubled an octave below

Four notes in the right hand, then the left hand doubles the top note an octave down. Five notes, both hands locked together, moving as one shape. This is the "locked hands" sound. (NK 2020-07-30 · 00:59–03:20)

Also taught as octave chords — the melody in octaves with a diatonic triad inside, the stride and Erroll Garner version of the same outer octave: see Octave chords in Stride.

Seventh block chords

Take a closed seventh chord and double its top note an octave below: B♭∆7 becomes A B♭ D F A. The half step at the bottom is the sound — a minor 7th puts a whole step there, and the shape reads as an ordinary block chord. (NK 2023-03-08 · 01:38–04:35)

B♭∆7 A B♭ D F A the basic shape moved intervallically D♭∆7 · E∆7 · D∆7 — the same structure on each root keep the half step m(∆7) · ∆7sus4 · ∆7sus2 B♭°∆7 A B♭ C♯ E A also reads A7♭9 — resolves to B♭∆7 add the 9 A B♭ C D F A a cluster at the bottom

Harmonize a melody by moving °∆7 shapes intervallically under it — D♭°∆7, B°∆7, E°∆7, D°∆7 … — and resolve to B♭∆; or voice every second note and double the melody in the left hand. Two more block colours: the same ∆7 in each hand an octave apart (neo-soul "stacked 7ths"), and a Dorian block chord, 1 ♭3 5 ♭7 1. (NK 2023-03-08 · 06:53–08:51; NK 2020-06-11 · 05:56–07:25; NK 2020-07-30 · 03:53–04:18)

Drop 2, properly

Drop 2 isn't a voicing — it's a spacing rule you apply to any four-note chord, in any inversion. Take the close-position chord, count down from the top, and drop the second voice an octave. Because you can start from any of the four inversions, every chord yields four drop-2 voicings — and each one puts a different chord tone on top.

Close position · the problem

C E G B inside a single octave. Fine at the top of the keyboard, mud below middle C, and it needs one hand to hold all four notes.

Drop 2 · the fix

Drop the G and the chord spans 16 semitones — just over an octave. That's the narrowest spacing that stays clear in the register you actually play in, and it splits naturally between two hands.

Four inversions, four melody notes

This is the part worth memorizing. You don't choose a drop-2 voicing by the chord — you choose it by which note you need on top. All four below are C∆7.

From root position · B on top

C E G B → G · C E B

From 1st inversion · C on top

E G B C → B · E G C

From 2nd inversion · E on top

G B C E → C · G B E

From 3rd inversion · G on top

B C E G → E · B C G

The counting trap. "Second voice from the top" means second in the inversion you started from — not the chord's 5th. From root position you drop the G; from first inversion you drop the B; from second, the C; from third, the E. Get this wrong and you'll produce the same voicing four times.

The same rule on dominant and minor

G7 · root position

G B D F → D · G B F

The tritone B–F ends up as the top two voices, which is why drop-2 dominants sound so pointed.

Dm7 · root position

D F A C → A · D F C

Identical procedure. The rule cares about the number of voices, not the chord quality.

Drop 2 & 4

drop the 2nd and 4th voices

C G E B — nearly two octaves. Use it when drop 2 still isn't wide enough, or when you want the bass genuinely separated from the colour.

Also taught on the sixth chords of the Barry engine: C6 as 6 3 5 1, moved up the C6-diminished scale; Cm6 as 6 ♭3 5 1. (NK 2021-12-17 · 02:16–04:30; NK 2022-11-27 · 17:19–17:52)

Mixing the structures: sugar chords

Close, drop 2 and drop 3 on one line of melody, mixed rather than kept apart: the outer voices move in contrary motion and a tenor counter-line appears without being written. (OS clip Sugar Chords · 04:39–16:56)

Tune On Green Dolphin Street, bars 9–12 in E♭: Fm7 – B♭7 – E♭ Notes A♭6-diminished over Fm7 and the first half of B♭7 · B minor-6 diminished for the altered notes · E♭6-diminished over E♭ Mix drop 3 → close → drop 2 under a rising melody, then the reverse

Each structure has its register: close when the hands are near, drop 2 as they spread — it delivers a tenth between the top note and the dropped one — and drop 3 lower still, for the tenor range. The root stays free in the left hand.

Why you learn all four: voice leading

Pick the form whose top note is the melody you want, then pick the next chord's form that's nearest. Done properly a whole ii–V–I moves by six semitones in total, spread across two inner voices, while the melody note holds or falls by a step.

melody on F: Dm7 D A C F top F G7 D G B F top F — holds; F is ♭7 of both chords C∆7 C G B E top E — falls a semitone total movement across all three chords: 6 semitones

All four chains — melody on C, D, F or A — are in the exercise player as Drop 2 · ii–V–I, steppable and transposable into any key. That is the drill: not the shapes on their own, but choosing a shape by its top note and then moving as little as possible.

The Barry Harris engine

Here's the part that makes block chords actually usable rather than a per-note puzzle. The sixth-diminished scale already alternates two chords — so you harmonize a scale by alternating them, and every melody note gets a voicing automatically.

The alternation

C D E F G A♭ A B ← C6-diminished C6 D°7 C6 D°7 C6 D°7 C6 D°7

Chord tones of C6 (C E G A) get a C6 inversion. Everything between them gets a D°7 inversion. That's the whole rule — no decisions per note.

Why it works

Because the two chords share no notes and together fill the eight-note scale, every step of the melody is covered, and consecutive voicings move by the smallest possible distance. The inner voices walk; nothing leaps. Harmonize a scale this way and the result sounds composed.

Same machinery for minor (Cm6 alternating with D°7) and for dominants (C7 alternating with D°7) — the formulas are up in the Barry Harris section. Add the melody note an octave below in the left hand and the Barry system becomes the Shearing sound. Also practised in the left hand alone (Bill Evans). (NK 2020-07-30 · 04:26–05:47; NK 2020-10-01 · 01:11–02:28)

The minor ladder: Cm6 and its diminished, up the scale

The minor version of the engine, worked out. Keep C in the left hand and walk a four-note right-hand shape up the C minor sixth-diminished scale — C D E♭ F G A♭ A B (1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 6 7) — every voice moving one scale note each time. The shapes alternate between only two chords: Cm6 in its four inversions, and one diminished seventh, B°7 — the same four notes as D°7, F°7 and A♭°7, and the rootless G7♭9, so the ladder is tonic and dominant taking turns. The tonic · Cm6

E♭ G A C over C

The first rung. Play the run walks all eight shapes over the held C.

The diminished · B°7

F A♭ B D over C

Every other rung is this one chord in a new inversion — the rootless G7♭9 inside C minor.

Naming each shape by its top note works for the diminished shapes, because they are one chord, but not for the Cm6 shapes: G A C E♭ is E♭6♯11 only with E♭ in the bass, and A C E♭ G is Aø7 — not A7♭5, which needs a C♯. The scale and its two chords are listed under The Barry Harris System; the left-hand-alone practice above is the Bill Evans habit.

Also taught as two-voice counterpoint: see Two voices from one scale in Barry Harris.

How to practice it

1 Play the C6-diminished scale up and down, one octave, right hand only. 2 Harmonize each note — C6 inversion on chord tones, D°7 inversion between. 3 Add the left hand doubling the top note an octave down. That's locked hands. 4 Do the same on the minor-sixth and dominant-seventh diminished scales. 5 Take a melody you know. Harmonize only the notes that fall on beats. 6 Break the lock — let the left hand drop out for a bar, then come back.

Step 6 matters more than it looks. Unbroken block chords for thirty-two bars is exhausting to listen to; the technique reads as an effect only when it starts and stops.

Also taught as sparse block chording: harmonize only the highest and lowest notes of a line, for an arranged sound. (NK 2020-07-30 · 06:03–07:06)

Rhythm Changes

The other form everyone knows.

After the blues, this is the most-played set of changes in jazz — the harmony of I Got Rhythm, and underneath dozens of bebop heads. Thirty-two bars, AABA: eight bars of turnaround, twice, then a bridge that is nothing but dominants moving around the cycle. Shown here in C; the standard key is B♭.

The shape

A · 8 bars

I–vi–ii–V, twice, then IV

A turnaround repeated, a trip to the IV in bars 5–6, and a setup for the repeat. Played twice.

B · 8 bars

III7 – VI7 – II7 – V7

Four dominants, two bars each, around the cycle of fifths. No ii chords, no resolution until the last bar.

A · 8 bars

as before, with an ending

The last A resolves instead of turning around — that's the only difference.

Why it's the best practice vehicle

The A section is one cell

Bars 1–4 are I–vi–ii–V and bars 3–4 repeat it. If you can play four bars of turnaround, you can play sixteen of the thirty-two bars. Practice the cell, not the tune.

Target chain through the turnaround: C6 → E or A A7 → C♯ or G Dm7 → F or C G7 → B or F

The bridge is a cycle drill

Eight bars of dominants moving in fourths, two bars each — enough time to state an idea and transpose it. Play one phrase through all four chords, changing only the pitches.

Begin each arpeggio on the 3rd: E7 → G♯ A7 → C♯ D7 → F♯ G7 → B Then anticipate each new chord on the & of 4.

At tempo, the A section moves two chords per bar, so there is no time to think in scales — you're playing guide tones and one rhythm. That constraint is the lesson.

Rhythm changes, made modern

Five ways to make B♭ rhythm changes sound modern, read from his keys. (NK 2020-12-03 · 01:04–11:15)

1 Bars 1–4 as a B♭ pedal: B♭13sus (B♭ | A♭ C E♭ G), alternating with "G♭ over B♭sus" (G♭ A♭ B♭ D♭ F); release with a ii–V–I into the IV 2 Over the sus: B♭ Mixolydian (= F Dorian), or B♭ minor blues — B♭ minor pentatonic plus E, the ♭5 3 Replace bars 1–4 with a ii–V cycle: F♯m7–B7 | Em7–A7 | Dm7–G7 | Cm7–F7 → B♭ 4 The bridge as sus chords (Dsus, Gsus, Csus, Fsus) or as tritone subs: D9 D♭9 C9 B9 → B♭ 5 At the end of the bridge, B over F7; on the pedal, B♭ and E major triads as a pair, in inversions

A loop for the same territory: dominants falling in thirds, kept Mixolydian — B♭7 – G7 – E♭7 – C7. (NK clip dom progressions · 00:00–00:29)

Comping

What the other hand does.

Comping is a rhythm decision, not a voicing decision. The voicings on this page are already right; what makes a comp sound good is where the chords land and how much silence sits between them. Click the cells to build a two-bar pattern, or take one of these and edit it.

Rules that survive contact

Answer, don't accompany

Play in the soloist's gaps, not underneath their phrases. If you're both playing constantly, neither of you is heard.

Anticipate the change

Land the new chord on the & of 4 rather than the downbeat. It pulls the band forward; landing square pushes it back. (NK 2020-07-16 · 06:05–07:49)

Repeat, then break

Establish a pattern for two or four bars so it registers, then disrupt it. A comp with no pattern is noise; one that never breaks is wallpaper.

Three notes is plenty

A 3–7 shell plus one tension says everything. Full five-note voicings behind a soloist muddy the middle register where the horn lives.

Root, shell, pretty

When there is room — solo, or no bass — build up from that shell: the root, the shell (3rd and 7th), then two pretty notes from the 5, 9, 11 and 13. B♭∆7: B♭ | D A | C F. (OS clip maness root shell pretty · 00:33–00:57)

Stay out of the way

Keep voicings between roughly C3 and C5. Below that you fight the bass; above it you fight the melody.

Solo piano is different

With no bass or drums you own the time. Comp sparser than you think, and let the left hand state roots on 1 and 3 more often than you would in a trio. (NK 2022-01-09 · 01:08–05:58) More in Solo Piano.

A rhythm ladder for the left hand

One chord — rootless C∆9, E G B D over a C bass — and a ladder of rhythms: the left hand alone with a clap or a snap, then under a scale, then under improvisation. Count the "ands" aloud. (NK 2020-07-16 · 01:23–07:49)

Alone whole notes · 2 & 4 · &1 · &2 · &3 · &4 · &2 + &4 · &1 + &4 Under a scale the same, under right-hand eighths on C major; then hemiolas Under a solo whole notes · 2 & 4 · &1 + &3 · a dotted-quarter hemiola

When the right-hand line runs down into the chord, drop the chord's top note or two rather than revoicing.

Tension over a static chord

Under a held C∆7, move the left hand against the bass, then resolve. Read from his keys. (NK 2020-09-03 · 01:07–04:40)

Half-step pivot the 3-6-9 shape on C (E A D) → on D♭ (F B♭ E♭) and back Over the C bass C – D♭ – E♭ – D♭ Minor-third shifts E A D → G C F → B♭ E♭ A♭ → C♯ F♯ B → home iv over I F minor (F A♭ C D) over a C–G bass

Also taught on a long dominant: under a stretch of C7 (left hand E B♭ D, right hand C G C), add its V — G7♯9♭13 over G, left hand F B E♭ (each note up a half step), right hand E♭ B♭ E♭ (up a minor third) — and come back. Over a C bass the B would clash; the bass line goes to G. (OS clip maness warmup spread voicings · 00:00–00:52)

Five-note sets: the Magic Voicing System

One five-note structure per chord family, learned with its inversions, so the top note can move melodically while the hands stay in one place — no repeated notes and no big spreads. (OS workbook p.1–10)

The home voicing is 3 6 | 9 5 1 over B♭. Rotating a pentatonic voicing through its own scale is the same rule as Kellman’s pentatonic cycle; the altered set is the triad pairs over a shell. Gospel’s comping habits — the walk-up, the sus V, the grace note — are in Gospel.

Solo Piano

The whole band in two hands.

With no bass and no drums, one player carries the bass line, the harmony, the melody and the time. These are working methods for that job: how the left hand stands in for a bassist, how inner voices move under a held melody, and textures borrowed from other music. The comping rules are in Comping (Solo piano is different); the older left hand is in Stride & Ragtime; melodies voiced as chords are in Block Chords.

Three hands: bass, harmony, melody

Split the hands into three jobs: the left pinky (with the fourth finger) holds the bass, the right fourth and fifth fingers the melody, and the six fingers in between fill and move. He attributes the name, tentatively, to Fred Hersch. (NK 2021-07-11 · 01:10–01:57; NK 2021-11-06 · 04:06–05:51)

1 Hold bass and melody; move the inner fingers in eighth notes — up, down, then varied, pedal down 2 Diatonic inner motion (Bill Evans): the ♭7 ♭3 5 triad of Fm7 — E♭ A♭ C — stepped up F Dorian, each note to the next scale note 3 An inner melody in octaves under a held top note: over E♭ with G on top, B (♯5) → C … D → B♭ (5) 4 Passing chords for motion on a V–I: B♭13 → B♭7♭9♯11 → E9♯11 (the tritone sub, a half step above) → E♭∆7 5 Roll chords up or down in time; roll both hands at once

Steps 2–5: (NK 2023-03-27 · 03:10–07:07; NK 2020-10-01 · 08:04–09:16; NK 2021-07-11 · 02:03–07:40). Practise it on a ballad: the substitutions first, then the inner motion.

The left hand without a bassist

The ear needs roots, so the left hand gives them — not always as a single note, and not always on the beat. His example tune is "It Could Happen to You": E♭∆ → Gø7 → C7 → Fm → Aø7 → D7 → E♭∆. (NK 2023-06-15 · 01:01–05:19; NK 2022-01-09 · 01:08–08:31)

Walking, for one player. First a two-feel — a bass note every two beats: roots where chords change, chord tones or chromatic passing tones between. Then a note per beat: chord tones on 1 and 3, the root landing on the change — over F7 → B♭: 1 ♭7 6 5 → B♭. Swing devices: hit the third triplet; hop the octave.

The gallop

A left-hand engine from Brad Mehldau: the root in eighth notes, then the 9 above it so the two thumbs sit a small interval apart, then a galloping rhythm. (NK 2021-12-26 · 01:09–07:49)

1 The root in steady eighths through the changes (All the Things You Are) 2 Add the 9 above the root — the right thumb takes the ♭3/10th; or play the 10th itself 3 The gallop: 1, 2-and, 3-and, 4 … 4 Variation: 1 9 5 9, the 5 with the index 5 Melody with the right pinky, then inner melodies with fingers 2–3, then improvise the top

The piano as an orchestra

Fill the melody's gaps in a different register; put the melody in the left hand and the chords in the right; use two-handed runs that outline the changes as fills; on a ballad, arpeggiate the left hand under a plain melody (Chopin, Mehldau) or spread wider from a low bass in open intervals such as tenths; and mix rooted shapes with rootless voicings so the bass motion is heard. (NK 2020-09-24 · 02:08–10:26)

Erroll Garner's ballad left hand is the same idea: the voicing arpeggiated — E♭ as 1 3 5 6 (E♭ G B♭ C), then B♭m7, E♭7. (NK 2020-08-27 · 10:25–12:21)

Three left-hand lines, read from his keys with his fingerings, that double as starting points for a tune. (NK 2023-04-06 · 01:27–05:30)

Bossa for one player

Left hand: root and 5th in the bossa rhythm, moving by fifths or by major sevenths — F∆9 (F | C G A C) ↔ G♭∆9 (G♭ | D♭ A♭ B♭ D♭). Right hand split: thumb, index and middle play syncopated chords while fingers 4–5 hold the melody. Start by holding a melody note, then add the chord rhythms, then vary them. (NK 2021-05-13 · 01:16–04:45)

One texture from the classics

Take one bar you love, not a whole piece, and drill it until it is yours: move it in half steps, whole steps, minor thirds, then voice a melody with it. (NK 2022-04-24 · 02:00–19:53; NK 2022-05-08 · 00:53–14:38; NK 2022-05-22 · 02:15–10:16)

Intros, Endings & Tags

How to start and how to stop.

The two moments an audience actually notices, and the two most players never practice. All of these are formulas — learn four and you can begin or end any standard without discussing it first.

Intros

Vamp on the last four

| Em7 A7 | Dm7 G7 | ×2

Take the tune's final four bars and loop them until the head starts. Works on almost anything, requires no arrangement, and tells the band exactly where you are.

The pedal

G in the bass, everything moves above

Hold the dominant in the bass and move upper voices freely over it. Tension with no obligation — release into bar 1 of the head whenever you want.

Rubato from the last phrase

final 2 bars, out of time

Play the tune's last two bars freely, slowing into a fermata on the V — then count off. The ballad default.

Endings

The tag

repeat the last 4 bars ×3, then end

The universal ending. Loop the final cadence three times — the third time usually goes up a half step or gets more altered — then resolve. Everyone knows to stop on the third pass.

♭II7 into the tonic

D♭7♯11 → C6/9

The tritone sub as a final gesture. Both guide tones fall a half step into the tonic, so it lands with no ambiguity about being over.

The 6/9

C6/9 — C E G A D

Don't end on a ∆7 — the major 7th still wants to move. A 6/9 has no leading tone and no tension left, which makes it the safest final chord — unless you want mystery: a Bill Evans ending below closes on the I°7. Two endings keep a tension on purpose: C7♯11 at the end of a blues, and D/C — C Lydian — on a ballad. (NK 2020-07-02 · 09:13–09:45; NK 2023-07-03 · 08:06–08:26)

A Bill Evans ending

A ballad ending in F after Jack Reilly’s The Harmony of Bill Evans (the close of “I Fall in Love Too Easily”): the half-diminished chord on the ♭5 walks down to a 3–6–2–5, the bass falling chromatically B B♭ A A♭ G before the C — and the last chord is not the tonic major. (OS clip Bill Evans Chords · 02:16–12:31)

Plain Bø7 – B♭m7 – Am7 – D7alt – Gm7 – C7 – F Bill Evans Bø7 – B♭m11 – Am7 – D♭7♯11/A♭ – Gm13 – C7sus → C7(♯11♭9) – F°7
ChordVoicingWhy
Bø7root, shell and 5ththe ♭5, a tritone from home, with the tonic F on top
B♭m11left hand B♭ E♭ A♭ (1 11 ♭7, fourths) · right hand D♭ F (3 5)the iv made minor

F°7—a bit of mystery instead of a resolution

Ending on the I°7 is the deliberate alternative to the 6/9: the 6/9 closes the door, the diminished leaves it ajar. Practise the first three bars as a loop at ballad tempo — roll the tenths if they do not reach, outside notes first and then fill in — then a slow two-feel, in F, G, A♭ and B♭; the same cadence also opens a ballad.

The Coltrane tag

Worth learning on its own: instead of looping I–vi–ii–V, descend by major thirds on the way back.

Standard tag | C6 A7 | Dm7 G7 | ×3 Coltrane tag | C6 E♭7 | A♭6 B7 | E6 G7 | C6 | Each new tonic is a major 3rd below the last — C, A♭, E, back to C.

Same eight bars, same destination, three tonal centers instead of one. Play it slowly the first hundred times.

The ii–V–I Lab

One cadence, twelve roads home.

The same three bars — relit twelve ways. Each tab is a substitution path. Under every chord: the NewJazz hand grips first — left-hand grip from the simulator, then the right-hand grips — and then the scales, with any scale that has the same notes as another shown in parentheses, e.g. D minor pentatonic (F major pentatonic), G Lydian dominant (D melodic minor). The keyboard under every chord shows the featured pentatonic in red, with the chord tones it sits on in amber underneath.

Substitution Finder

Type a chord, get its exits.

Enter any chord and get the standard substitutions — tritone, diminished, related ii, altered, and the reharmonizations particular to its quality. Every result is playable.

Field Recording · 1964

Herbie on Stella.

Three arpeggiated runs from Stella by Starlight — Miles Davis, My Funny Valentine (live, 1964), in the tune's key of B♭. Each run is one collection of notes, cycled up the keyboard several times and then thrown an octave higher before it falls back.

The three arpeggios

Checked against a MIDI transcription of the piano. It is an AI separation, so it is a guide rather than proof — but it confirms all three note collections exactly, gives their order, and shows the shape of each run. Play the run plays a cleaned version of the transcription at its own speed; Half speed slows it down for the hands.

1 · Over G7alt

A♭ B♭ C♭ E♭ F G

E♭ hexatonic major — 1 2 3 4 5 ♭6 of E♭. Over G it reads ♭9 ♯9 3 ♭13 ♭7 1: a complete altered dominant, and exactly the Santangelo move: G7alt with E♭ hexatonic.

The run: A♭ B♭ C♭ E♭ F G upward, about a dozen times, then the same cell an octave up to G and down E♭ C♭ A♭ G F E♭.

2 · Over Cm7

A B♭ C D E♭ F G

The B♭ major collection, which over the C the transcription hears in the bass is C Dorian — 1 9 ♭3 11 5 13 ♭7. The plainest choice of the three: the ii of the home key, played straight.

The run: seven notes up from A, again and again, then a climb to G and a scale back down to A.

3 · Over A♭7

A♭ B♭ C D E♭ F G♭

A♭ Lydian dominant — 1 2 3 ♯11 5 6 ♭7, the 4th mode of E♭ melodic minor. The D is the ♯11.

The run: A♭ B♭ C D E♭ F cycling upward; the G♭ (the ♭7) only appears at the top of the climb.

In B♭, bars 17–22 of the form: G7(♯5) | G7 | Cm7 | Cm7 | A♭7 | A♭7 G7alt E♭ hexatonic major ♭9 ♯9 3 ♭13 ♭7 1 Cm7 B♭ major (C Dorian) 1 9 ♭3 11 5 13 ♭7 A♭7 E♭ melodic minor A♭ Lydian dominant B♭ · E♭ · F run through all three — the key's root, 4th and 5th never leave.

How sure is the placement? The order of the runs in the transcription, the C it hears under the second one, and the key of B♭ all line up with bars 17–22 — the transcription caught no bass under the first and third runs, so those two chords are inferred from the form. An earlier reading labelled the same three collections B♭sus4♭9/13, D7♭9/A and A♭6/♯11, reading them against other roots. One correction from v3.7: that page said the second run had "no alteration" over D7♭9. Over a D it would leave out F♯, the chord's 3rd — the C bass is what makes it plain.

Other devices · unverified

+

Earlier notes on this solo. The transcription doesn't confirm them — what it covers is the three runs above — so treat these as devices Herbie uses rather than as a transcription of these bars.

Quartal sus sweep

G pedal in the left hand, a quartal stack in the right — G13sus(9) — arpeggiated, then the whole shape slid up a half step.
LH G — D — A
RH C — F — B — E
Arp G C F B E A D · then up ½ → A♭ D♭ G♭ B F B♭ E♭

Add-9 planing

Two add9 voicings with no third, moved chromatically.
E♭(add9, no 3): E♭ F B♭ G
E(add9, no 3): E F♯ B G♯

Polychord over a pedal

G held in the bass; Cm9 above it, then Fm9 — the upper structure moves while the bass stays.
LH G · G
RH C E♭ G D → F A♭ C G

Lydian cascade

A♭maj13(♯11) rolled across both hands; the D natural is the ♯11.
A♭ — C — E♭ — G — D — F

Altered dominant arpeggio

A G7alt arpeggio pointing back to the tonic.
G — B — F — A♭ — D♭ — E♭ (R · 3 · ♭7 · ♭9 · ♭5/♯11 · ♯9)
Time & Phrasing

The part that isn't notes.

Everything else on this page answers which notes. None of it answers when — and when is what makes a line sound like jazz rather than like a scale being demonstrated. A correct phrase with square rhythm sounds like an exercise; a plain phrase with good time sounds like music.

Rhythm decides whether it sounds like jazz. Target notes decide whether it follows the changes. Scales, arpeggios, and chromatics are only the route between the targets.

Start off the beat

The single most common reason a line sounds stiff: every phrase begins on beat 1 and ends at the bar line, so the solo gets chopped into one-measure scale demonstrations. (NK 2023-01-08 · 04:16–05:46)

Enter late

& of 2 · & of 3 · & of 4

Over | Dm7 | G7 | C∆7 |, begin on the & of 2 in the first bar, run through the G7, and land on beat 2 of the C∆7. One sentence across three chords.

Anticipate

B on the & of 4 → G7

Play a note belonging to the next chord just before it arrives. One note is enough on the gig — switching the whole scale early sounds like a mistake rather than a lean. As a drill the opposite works: run the next chord's scale a beat, two beats, a whole chord early; the clash trains the ear to hear where the changes are going. (NK 2022-07-31 · 02:36–08:12)

Delay the resolution

G7 → C∆7, resolve on beat 2

Let the dominant spill a beat into the tonic bar. The harmony changes on beat 1; the melody catches up on beat 2 or 3. Instant forward motion.

One rhythmic cell, many pitches

A motif is a rhythm, not a melody. Keep the rhythm fixed and change the notes to follow the changes — the listener hears one idea developing instead of eleven unrelated ones. (NK 2023-07-11 · 08:37–14:01)

Cells worth owning

Three eighths + a quarter Quarter + two eighths Triplet pickup into the downbeat 3 + 3 + 2 across the bar Dotted-quarter groupings in 4/4 Repeated note + syncopated tail

Six ways to develop one

Repeat it on the next chord Displace it by one eighth note Shorten the ending Extend the final note Answer it an octave lower Invert the contour, keep the rhythm

Phrase lengths that cross the bar

If phrases are 2 and 4 bars long, they align with the form and the solo sounds like a worksheet. Odd lengths force the line across the harmonic seams.

Practice phrases lasting 3 beats · 5 beats · 6 beats · 1½ bars · 2 bars + a pickup. A five-beat phrase over one-bar chords crosses the bar line automatically — you can't play it square.

Leave space

Silence is where the harmony and the rhythm you just played actually register. A solo with no rests gives the listener nowhere to stand.

Bars 1–2 statement Bar 3, beats 1–2 answer Bar 3, beats 3–4 silence Bar 4 pickup into the next statement

On solo piano, the left hand can take the answer: a 3–7 shell, a quartal stab, or an anticipatory chord on the & of 4 — then get out of the way again.

Change one variable

The most common practice mistake is changing rhythm, harmony, register, and substitution at once, which makes it impossible to tell what improved.

Keep the rhythm fixed; change the harmony. Keep the harmony fixed; change the rhythm. Keep the notes fixed; displace the accents. Keep the phrase fixed; begin it on a different subdivision. Keep the target fixed; approach it by a different route.

One lick, many lines

Learn one lick deeply, then take it apart and rebuild it, rather than collecting dozens. (NK 2023-05-14 · 01:55–08:53; NK 2023-02-07 · 05:55–16:48)

1 Hear it first: sing each note, check it at the piano, then sing the whole lick and land it — away from the piano too 2 Take it apart: over E♭m7 → A♭7 → D♭, an E♭m9 arpeggio and E♭ Dorian down → an enclosure with the ♭9 and ♯9 → the D♭ blues scale (read from his keys) 3 Rebuild from the recipe: arpeggiate up instead of down, change the rhythm, keep the scale order 4 Transpose by degree (it starts on the 4 of the ii), then random keys, then up in half steps 5 Fit it to a tune you know cold (All the Things You Are); start it on the "and" of 1 6 Spread the repetition: five times on day 1, four on day 2, down to one; then improvise with it forced in

Five kinds of line

Five styles of improvised line, and when each one helps. (NK 2023-08-22 · 01:25–15:41)

StyleWhat it isWhen
bebopchord tones on 1 and 3, reached by approach notes and enclosureson bebop tunes; to open a solo
pentatonicfive notes reordered across octaves — open, fourth-basedto raise the intensity; on modal tunes, side-stepping the chord by a half or whole step
hexatonictwo triads as one six-note scale — C + D, or C minor + D minorcolour over a static chord
sequentialone cell moved by a fixed interval, whatever the keyto build tension, modal or over a ii–V–I
open intervallicwide, arpeggiated lines with no clustered chromaticismlater in a solo, to use the range

Swing is accent and placement

Same notes, same rhythm: accent the offbeats instead of the beats and the line swings. Then start and end phrases on the "ands", and find your own ratio between straight eighths and triplets. (NK 2023-01-08 · 01:18–10:08)

1 Improvise with every offbeat accented — exaggerated at first 2 Start and end lines on the "ands" 3 With a play-along, move slowly from straight eighths towards triplets and back; listen to where great players put theirs — often nearer straight 4 Record MIDI to a grid and check where your notes fall

Oscar Peterson's feel: lean toward the triplet and release the keys quickly — light and bouncy — without accenting the third triplet. (NK 2021-01-21 · 01:57–04:35)

The Reharmonization Lab

Twelve bars. Another way through.

Enter any progression. The lab preserves its harmonic destination, then proposes alternative routes — with the reason, the scale, and the voice-leading logic behind every change.

Use spaces between chords inside a bar: Dm7 G7alt. Use % to repeat the previous bar.

Ready
The alternatives will appear here. Click any chord to audition it.

Secondary dominant to tritone sub

A warmup that walks the whole scale and ends somewhere much further out than it started. Three passes over the same eight chords: plain, then with a secondary dominant in front of each, then with every one of those dominants re-read as its tritone substitution. (OS clip tritone sub warmup · 00:00–00:47)

A 7♭13 and the 9♯11 a tritone away are the same four notes. Voice the dominant as 1 · 3 · ♭13 · ♭7, then move the bass down a tritone and leave your right hand exactly where it is — the root you were holding becomes the ♯11.
TargetIts V7♭13Those four notesRe-read over the tritone
C∆9G7♭13G B E♭ FD♭9♯11
Dm9A7♭13A D♭ F GE♭9♯11
Em7B7♭13B E♭ G AF9♯11
F∆9C7♭13C E A♭ B♭G♭9♯11
G9D7♭13D G♭ B♭ CA♭9♯11
Am9E7♭13E A♭ C DB♭9♯11
as the dominant 1 · 3 · ♭13 · ♭7 as the tritone sub ♯11 · ♭7 · 9 · 3 — identical notes, renamed Every substitute lands a half step above its target, so the bass descends by semitone: D♭→C E♭→D F→E G♭→F A♭→G B♭→A

The ♭13 is what makes the trick work. A plain 7th chord doesn't convert cleanly — it's the ♭13 that becomes the substitute's 9th, and the original root that becomes its ♯11. All three passes are in the exercise player as Sec dom → tritone sub, where the right hand is visibly unchanged between pass two and pass three. The Substitution Finder will do the same conversion on any chord you type.

Also taught as target practice: from C∆7 to each diatonic chord by its dominant a fifth above (A7 → Dm7), then by the tritone sub from the other side of the circle, sussed (E♭7sus → Dm7); the vii is skipped. (OS clip target practice · 00:00–01:03)

One melody note, a moving bass

The real-time reharmonization drill: hold one melody note on top and move the bass by half steps, finding a chord for every bass note. Then whole steps, then patterns — up a half step, down, up, up — then a new melody note. (NK 2021-06-18 · 02:30–05:42; NK 2022-06-26 · 01:11–05:40)

MelodyBassA chord that keeps it
FFany F chord — the melody is the root
FG♭G♭∆7, G♭∆9, G♭m(∆7) — the melody is the ∆7
FGGm11 — the melody is the ♭7
GEEm11, C(sus2)/E, E7♯9♯5
GF♯E minor over F♯

The holes it exposes are voicings you can't find in every key — practise them intervallically, as in One minor-11 shape — or sounds you can't hear yet. The warm-up form: drone one top note while the bass walks up and down by half steps, then fill the middle. (NK 2022-06-26 · 05:40–06:49; NK clip chord warmup1 · 00:04–00:13)

Also taught with the roots falling in fifths: one top note, E, becomes in turn 3, ∆7, ♯11, ♭9, ♯5, ♯9, ♭7, 4, 1, 5, 9 and 13, with only root, 3rd and 7th underneath; or as an open game — keep one top note and find every chord that holds it. (OS clip osj keeping note on top · 00:03–01:25; OS clip maness warmup with top note · 00:00–00:44)

Three ways to reharmonize in real time

On "Night and Day": three techniques you can use without stopping the tune. (NK 2022-07-03 · 00:58–06:47)

1 Planing one voicing, 1 5 9 3 7, with the melody always its ∆7 — the whole shape follows the melody (soon overused) 2 Repeated note a different chord under each repetition of the same melody note 3 Bass up a scale the bass climbs F Dorian under the melody: Fm11 → E♭/G (4 on top) → A♭ → B♭sus → C∆9 the sus a whole step below resolving to the major

Resolutions held together by voice leading

Almost any resolution works if the voices move by small steps and keep common tones; avoid big jumps between voicings. Five non-functional ones, read from his keys: (NK 2021-08-08 · 01:36–06:56)

MoveExample
major from a half step aboveD∆13♯11 → D♭∆9
minor 11 to the major a half step belowB♭m11 → A
major to the major a minor 3rd belowF∆(13) → D
minor 11 up a minor 3rdA♭m11 → Bm11
13sus a whole step below the majorD13sus4 → E∆ — top B held, E → D♯, G → G♯

The same sus resolution runs through the scale-walk above (B♭sus → C∆9) and the chromatic approach B♭13sus → G(add2)/B → C∆ in Warmups.

Perfect or plagal: by fifths or by fourths

Take C → Am and approach each chord two ways: from a fifth above (perfect) or from a fourth above (plagal) — then back up one more step each way. (OS clip perfect and plagal · 00:00–00:56)

Perfect E7 → Am · G7 → C back a step: B7 → E7 → Am · D7 → G7 → C Plagal Dm7 → Am · F → C back a step: … → Dm7 → Am · B♭ → F → C

Also taught as stacking fourths: from C to Am through Dm, home through F; then put another fourth in front of each — Gm – Dm – Am and B♭ – F – C — and again: Cm – Gm – Dm – Am and E♭ – B♭ – F – C. (OS clip Stacking 4ths · 00:00–00:44)

One ii–V–I, five levels

Dm – G7 – C, reharmonized in five steps from the textbook to the non-functional. Levels 1 and 2 — the backdoor and tritone sub, and the descending ii–Vs — are in Reharmonization Recipes in Reference; levels 3 to 5 are below, read from his keys. (NK 2023-09-02 · 05:13–10:34)

Level 3 · diatonic soul E7♯9 → Am9 → Gm9 → C9 → F∆9 → Dm11 → C(add9) a ii–V–I into F, then home to C Level 4 · neo-soul D/F♯ → G9sus → E/G♯ → Am(add9) → B♭13sus → Gsus2/B → C bass F♯ G G♯ A B♭ B C — the 3rds in the bass act as secondary dominants Level 5 · sequential Dm11 → Fm11 → A♭m11 → B♭sus → C one m11 shape up in minor thirds, then sus to home

Level 5 is One minor-11 shape, any root used as a progression.

Also in graded settings for gospel, one melody harmonized three ways: see One melody, three settings in Gospel.

Passing chords a half step away

"Body and Soul": slip in the chord a half step above or below the target, reach it by a diatonic walk-up, or delay the landing. The passing chord still has to fit the melody note, and a bass line that makes sense ties the substitutions together. (NK 2022-01-30 · 02:28–14:23)

E♭m → B9♯11 → B♭7♭9 the melody F is the ♯11 of B A13♭9 → A♭13♭9 → D♭13 a half step, then a tritone E♭m walked up E♭ Dorian, then A♭sus → A♭13 C → F over a diatonic bass, with a half-step chord before the F end of an A section: the majors a half step above and below, then D♭

A bass walk in the same spirit: Am → E(add9)/G♯ → Gm, the bass A A♭ G (Larry Grenadier under Brad Mehldau). (NK 2021-02-18 · 07:26–08:57)

In gospel the half-step move becomes a vocabulary — moo chords and ♯9 dominants from below: see Approach chords in Gospel.

A whole tune as a journey

"Christmas Time Is Here" reharmonized as a path from point A to point B rather than a chord for every melody note: start on the original chord, step off and come back, travel further, and finish somewhere new. (NK 2020-12-24 · 01:11–14:43)

1 Start on the original (C∆9), step off briefly (Am11 → F), come back 2 Put a chord on a non-melody beat as a pause (Em11) 3 Let a strong bass line carry chords that each fit the melody — the "waterfall": E♭ F D♭ A G♭ D B under A♭∆9, B/F, D♭∆7, B/A, G♭∆7, D alt, B13♯11 4 Avoid the expected resolution; restate an earlier idea in a new key 5 End elsewhere: the last A moves up to B
Warmups

Warmups that go somewhere.

Sixteen drills that aren't finger exercises — each one is a harmonic idea you practise with your hands until it stops needing thought. Seven of them are steppable and transposable in the exercise player: the moo chord warmup, secondary dominant and diminished, the oblique warmup, Barry Harris, the Maness key change, secondary dominant to tritone sub, and the Mountain.

The moo chord warmup

Two shapes, alternating. A ∆7 with its 7th at the bottom of the right hand, then a 2–5–1 built on the chord a fifth below, voiced over that chord's 3rd. The right hand moves one note at a time throughout. (OS clip moo chords · 00:00–00:31)

Shape one · ∆7

7 · 3 · 5 over the root

C∆7 as B–E–G over a C bass. Putting the 7th lowest is what gives the shape its particular ache.

Shape two · the 2 chord

2 · 5 · 1 over the 3rd

G(2)/B — A–D–G over a B bass. From the C∆7, two notes move by step and the G stays put.

Then drop a whole step

B♭∆7

A–D–F. The A and D are held from the chord before; only the top note falls. That economy is the whole exercise.

one cell: X∆7 · (X−5)(2)/3rd · (X−2)∆7 · (X−7)(2)/3rd on C: C∆7 · G(2)/B · B♭∆7 · F(2)/A on D: D∆7 · A(2)/C♯ · C∆7 · G(2)/B on E: E∆7 · B(2)/D♯ · D∆7 · A(2)/C♯ on F♯: F♯∆7 · C♯(2)/E♯· E∆7 · B(2)/D♯ on A♭: A♭∆7 · E♭(2)/G · G♭∆7 · D♭(2)/F on B♭: B♭∆7 · F(2)/A · A♭∆7 · E♭(2)/G pass 2, a half step up: on D♭: D♭∆7 · A♭(2)/C · B∆7 · F♯(2)/A♯ on E♭: E♭∆7 · B♭(2)/D · D♭∆7 · A♭(2)/C on F: F∆7 · C(2)/E · E♭∆7 · B♭(2)/D on G: G∆7 · D(2)/F♯ · F∆7 · C(2)/E on A: A∆7 · E(2)/G♯ · G∆7 · D(2)/F♯ on B: B∆7 · F♯(2)/A♯· A∆7 · E(2)/G♯
The cell climbs a whole step each time, so its six starting points are C D E F♯ A♭ B♭ — one whole-tone scale, six of the twelve keys. Then, as the video says, take the whole thing up a half step: the second pass starts on D♭ and covers the other six. (OS clip moo chords · 00:00–00:31)

Inside each cell the second ∆7 is a whole step below the first, and the next cell starts a whole step above — so the roots go down a whole step and then up a major third, a net climb of a whole step per cell. Both passes, forty-eight chords, are in the exercise player as Moo chord warmup.

Also taught as a chromatic approach into I: B♭13sus → G(add2)/B → C∆, bass B♭ B C — after Lyle Mays: 1 2 5 over its own 3rd, resolving up. (NK 2021-01-28 · 01:11–02:57; NK 2022-06-21 · 03:45–06:18)

A Steely Dan mu needs the 2 and the 3 side by side; the spread form with the 3rd in the bass is the Open Studio moo. (OS clip Moo Chords advanced · 00:00–00:45)

Secondary dominant and diminished

Walk the scale, and between every pair of chords insert the V7 of the one you're heading to — in first inversion, so its 3rd sits in the bass a half step below the target. Then raise that dominant's root a half step and it becomes a diminished seventh, which falls into the next chord by semitone. (OS clip secondary dominants and secondary diminished · 00:03–00:30)

The dominant

A7/C♯

A7 is the V7 of Dm. Put its 3rd — C♯ — in the bass and you're already a semitone under the destination.

Raise the root

C♯°7

The A moves up to B♭ — one note — and the chord is a diminished seventh. It's the rootless A7♭9.

Fall a semitone

Dm7

C♯ → D in the bass and you've arrived at the next rung of the scale.

C∆7 → A7/C♯ → C♯°7 → Dm7 Dm7 → B7/D♯ → D♯°7 → Em7 Em7 → C7/E → E°7 → F∆7 F∆7 → D7/F♯ → F♯°7 → G∆7 G∆7 → E7/G♯ → G♯°7 → Am7 Am7 → G7/B → B°7 → C∆7 bass: C C♯ C♯ D D♯ D♯ E E E F F♯ F♯ G G♯ G♯ A B B C
Every one of those diminished chords is the dominant before it with its root raised a half step — which is to say it is that dominant's rootless ♭9. You are not learning six diminished chords. You are learning one move.

Two details worth noticing. The V degree is written G∆7 rather than G7, because here each rung is a local resting place rather than a dominant — the only dominants in the exercise are the inserted ones. And the walk skips the vii°, going straight from Am7 to the G7/B that delivers you home; that's the one place the bass moves a whole step instead of a half. Full nineteen-chord version in the exercise player as Sec dom & diminished; the same device appears as a one-line recipe under Substitutions & Passing Chords, and the diminished-as-rootless-♭9 identity is worked out in Special Scales.

Also taught in reverse: lower one note of a diminished seventh a half step and it becomes a dominant on that note — F♯°7 → B7/F♯, in Fm → B7/F♯ → Gm → C7 → Fm. (NK 2023-01-24 · 10:16–11:03)

Oblique warmup · both hands together

Hold the right hand’s outer octave; the bass and the right hand’s middle voice walk together in tenths. In major, over held C octaves the bass climbs C–D–E–F and comes back; then the octaves move to G and the walk goes down to G and back up to C. In minor the climb uses E♭ and A♭, goes down through B♭ and A♭, and comes back up through A♮ and B♮ — natural minor going down, melodic minor going up. (OS clip oblique chord warmup · 00:04–00:26)

Major, C held

up to IV and back

Bass and middle voice climb C–D–E–F in tenths under the held C octave, and come back.

Major, G held

down to V and back

The octave moves to G; the walk goes down B–A–G and back up to B, then home to C.

Minor, C held

E♭ and A♭

The same climb in C minor: the middle voice runs E♭–F–G–A♭.

Minor, G held

down natural, up melodic

Down through B♭ and A♭ to G, then up through A♮ and B♮; C lands under the G octave with E♭ inside.

The plain pass is in even notes: the major C on a whole note, the walk in quarters, B, G and the minor C on half notes. The video then plays the same notes again with syncopation — anticipations, rests on the downbeats, ties across the bar — and the major pass ends on C–E♭–C to tip into minor; the warmup closes on two low-C eighth notes. (OS clip oblique chord warmup · 00:26–00:58) Both passes are in the exercise player as Oblique warmup: the plain pass, the syncopated pass whole, and its major and minor halves.

Barry Harris · hold the frame

The left hand holds the root, the right hand holds the 3rd in an octave, and between them both hands play the same four-note line an octave apart, four sixteenths to a chord. The line starts on the chord’s 7th, steps down to the next note of the scale, dips a half step and comes back. Where the scale’s 6th above the root is natural (I, ii, IV, V) that gives 7–6–♭6–6; where it is flat (iii, vi, vii) it gives ♭7–♭6–5–♭6. Same rule, two shapes. (OS clip barry harris warmup · 00:05–00:29)

in F, up the scale: F∆7 E D C♯ D Gm7 F E E♭ E Am7 G F E F B♭∆7 A G G♭ G C7 B♭ A A♭ A Dm7 C B♭ A B♭ Eø7 D C B C F∆7 (an octave up)

The hardest version tours four keys a minor third apart — F, A♭, B, D — and back to F. In each key it plays ii, I, ii, iii, and the iii slides up a half step to become the ii of the next key. So Am7 and A♭∆7 share one line, G–F–E–F: it is ♭7–♭6–5–♭6 of Am7 and 7–6–♭6–6 of A♭∆7. (OS clip barry harris warmup · 00:36–00:52)

F: F∆7 · Gm7 · Am7 → A♭: B♭m7 · A♭∆7 · B♭m7 · Cm7 → B: C♯m7 · B∆7 · C♯m7 · D♯m7 → D: Em7 · D∆7 · Em7 · F♯m7 → F: Gm7 · ending

F∆7 → Gm7

I → ii in F

F∆7: E–D–C♯–D (7–6–♭6–6). Gm7: F–E–E♭–E (♭7–6–♭6–6).

Am7 → B♭m7

iii of F, up a half step to the ii of A♭

Am7: G–F–E–F (♭7–♭6–5–♭6). B♭m7: A♭–G–G♭–G (♭7–6–♭6–6).

A♭∆7 → B♭m7

I → ii in A♭

A♭∆7: G–F–E–F (7–6–♭6–6). B♭m7: A♭–G–G♭–G (♭7–6–♭6–6).

Cm7 → C♯m7

iii of A♭, up a half step to the ii of B

Cm7: B♭–A♭–G–A♭ (♭7–♭6–5–♭6). C♯m7: B–A♯–A–A♯ (♭7–6–♭6–6).

B∆7 → C♯m7

I → ii in B

B∆7: A♯–G♯–G–G♯ (7–6–♭6–6). C♯m7: B–A♯–A–A♯ (♭7–6–♭6–6).

D♯m7 → Em7

iii of B, up a half step to the ii of D

D♯m7: C♯–B–A♯–B (♭7–♭6–5–♭6). Em7: D–C♯–C–C♯ (♭7–6–♭6–6).

D∆7 → Em7

I → ii in D

D∆7: C♯–B–A♯–B (7–6–♭6–6). Em7: D–C♯–C–C♯ (♭7–6–♭6–6).

F♯m7 → Gm7

iii of D, up a half step to the ii of F

F♯m7: E–D–C♯–D (♭7–♭6–5–♭6). Gm7: F–E–E♭–E (♭7–6–♭6–6).

The ending

octave shifts on F

LH holds F3–D4–E4 for a dotted quarter. RH plays A4–D5–A5 and A5–D6–G6 as eighths, then holds A6–D7–G7 under 8va; on the & of 2 the LH drops to F1 under 8ba, tied to a half note. (OS clip barry harris warmup · 00:52–00:55)

Each keyboard shows the first chord of the pair — root and line in the left hand, the 3rd’s octave and the same line in the right — and plays both chords. In the exercise player, Barry Harris warmup has the diatonic run in F, each pair, the ending, and the whole tour with the ending. The root and outer octave sustain through each group of four; only the line repeats.

The other warmups

Maness key change

C → F, six ways

Six stages that grow one device at a time — common tone, secondary dominant, its ii, a secondary dominant for that, then a tritone sub — turning a bare C → F into a fully reharmonized approach. Each stage is audible as a single added idea. (OS clip maness warmup keychange · 00:00–00:49)

Step 1: C → F Step 2: + common tone — C → Am → F Step 3: + sec dom — C → Am → C7 → F Step 4: + ii of sec dom — C → Am → Gm7 → C7 → F Step 5: + sec dom of ii of sec dom — C → Am → D7/F♯ → Gm7 → C7 → F Step 6: + tritone sub — C → Am → E♭7 → D7 → Gm7 → C7 → F

The tritone-sub chromatic pivot — E♭7 (E♭ G B♭ D♭) into D7 (D F♯ A C).

Secondary dominant to tritone sub

walk the scale, then alter it twice

The diatonic sevenths of C, then a V7♭13 in front of each, then every one of those re-read as its tritone substitute — the right hand never moving, because the two chords are the same four notes. Worked out in the Reharmonization Lab.

Step 1: Drop-2 voicings with the root in the bass, up the scale (LH: 1-3, RH: 7-9-5) Step 2: Insert sec dom before each (LH: 1-♭7, RH: 3-♭6-1) Step 3: Move LH 1-♭7 to ♭5-♭7 — the sec dom becomes a tritone sub (LH: 1-3, RH: ♭7-9-♯11) Result: C∆9 → A7♭13 → Dm9 → B7♭13 becomes C∆9 → E♭9♯11 → Dm9 → F9♯11

The transformed sec dom — E♭9♯11 (LH: E♭ G, RH: D♭ F A).

The Mountain

Start on C. Each pass reaches one rung higher — ii, then iii, IV, V, vi — and walks back down the scale to C, with a secondary dominant in front of every chord: unaltered dominants into the major chords and into V, altered dominants into the minor ones. (OS clip mountain secondary dominants · 00:00–00:51)

Step 1 LH: 1-3 [ii7] → 1-7 [V7] → 1-3 [I∆7] Step 2 RH: 7-9-5 [ii7] → 3-6-9 [V7] → 7-9-5 [I∆7] Pass 1 C – G7 – C Pass 2 C – A7 – Dm7 – G7 – C Pass 3 C – B7 – Em7 – A7 – Dm7 – G7 – C Pass 4 C – C7 – F∆7 – B7 – Em7 – A7 – Dm7 – G7 – C Pass 5 C – D7 – G7 – C7 – F∆7 – B7 – Em7 – A7 – Dm7 – G7 – C Pass 6 C – E7 – Am7 – D7 – G7 – C7 – F∆7 – B7 – Em7 – A7 – Dm7 – G7 – C = I∆7 → V7/vi → vi7 → V7/V → V7 → V7/IV → IV∆7 → V7/iii → iii7 → V7/ii → ii7 → V7 → I∆7 Unaltered dominants (RH 3–6–9) → major and V. Altered dominants (RH 3–♭13–♭9) → minor. On the iii chord the RH is 7–1–5: E D B, not the F♯ a 9 would need.

V7 in C — LH G–F (1, ♭7), RH B–E–A (3, 6, 9).

A7 into Dm7 — LH A–G (1, ♭7), RH C♯–F–B♭ (3, ♭13, ♭9).

C over G, approached four ways

Some cadences are timeless: C/G → G7 → C. Walk up to the C/G four different ways and take each one through all twelve keys. (OS clip C over G warmup · 00:00–00:52)

Plain C/G – G7 – C Chromatic C – C7/E – F – F♯°7 – C/G – G7 – C Diatonic Dm7 – C/E – … up the scale – C/G – G7 – C 6-diminished Fm/D – E°7 – Fm6 – C/G – G7 – C · Fm6/C – Fm6/A♭ – C/G – G7 – C From above A♭7/E♭ – D♭/F – A♭/G♭ – C/G – G7, ending on A♭∆9

The from-above route is the most surprising: the chords come down from A♭ while the bass climbs E♭–F–G♭ into the G of C/G, and the cadence lands. The 6-diminished pass borrows the minor iv, as in the Barry Harris section.

More moo, and two voicing drills

Short warmups that put the moo chord in front of other chords, and two that drill one voicing idea. The first and last are read from the staff; for the middle three the video shows only the bass line, so they are given as progressions without keyboards.

Moo – V – I

a moo before every secondary ii

In C, drop 2 (LH root, RH 5 7 3) up the scale; then a secondary ii–V in front of each chord, skipping vii — Em7♭5 A7/C♯ Dm7, F♯m7♭5 B7/D♯ Em7 …; then, in front of each of those ii chords, a moo built on its own V with the 3rd in the bass a half step below: C∆7 · B(2)/D♯ · Em7♭5 · A7/C♯ · Dm7 · C♯(2)/E♯ · F♯m7♭5 … (OS clip maness warmup mu-v-i · 00:00–00:55)

Moo before each 7th

down the diatonic sevenths

In C, the diatonic sevenths downward — I, vii, vi, v … — with a moo in front of each: the add-9 triad, in the Open Studio form drop 2 with the 3rd in the bass. Then re-invert the moo in the right hand, bottom note to the top, for contrary motion. (OS clip maness warmup with moo chord · 00:00–00:55)

ii–V–I with moo

every inversion, in F

The ii–V–I in F in each inversion, with D7 placed around the Gm7; then every dominant seventh swapped for its moo, a triad add 9. (OS clip maness warmup ii-v-i with moo · 00:00–00:46)

One phrase, three structures

F6 – Gm7 – A♭°7 – F6

In F, tonic, ii7, ♭III°7, tonic and back — in close voicings, then drop 2, then spread (RH 1 5 1 over the close structure in the LH). Round the cycle of fourths. (OS clip maness warmup voicings · 00:00–00:46)

Locked-hands D°7

move only the outer octave

LH D, RH F A♭ B D. Move only the outer Ds up to the next note of C major, E, and back; the inner notes stay. Then the same on each inversion: F → G, A♭ → A, B → C. (OS clip Diminished7 exercise · 00:12–00:45)

For ballad arpeggios, skip root-position triads and sevenths: take a four-note voicing — E A B D, 3 13 7 9 of C∆7 — and carry it across the octaves. Building your own is under Making your own in Reference. (OS clip arpeggios · 00:05–00:37)

Ostinatos for hand independence

Put one hand on autopilot so the other is free. (NK 2021-03-25 · 02:25–11:14; NK 2021-04-01 · 00:50–08:55)

OstinatoIn C
left hand 1C F G C (1 4 5 1) in eighths
left hand 2two octaves of 1 4 5 in triplets — C F G C F G C, up and back
left hand 31 4 5 cells with "hops": 5 3 2 1, bring 5 up; at the top, hop the thumb
right hand 1pinky G in quarters, thumb in eighths, fingers 2–3 on C–D on the sixteenths
right hand 2C F G B♭ C under fingers 1–5: 5 4 3 2 1 2 3 4, rolling the forearm — compare the 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 grip in NewJazz
right hand 3the left hand’s “hops” pattern, moved to the right: 1 2 3 5, bring the thumb up, hop the pinky down — in C, 1 4 5 1, a Csus4 sound (NK 2021-04-01 · 03:35–05:13)
right hand 4C F A B♭ — a triad plus a half step, reshaped as you go
right hand 5fingers 5 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 5, rocking between pinky and thumb — G D G D … (NK 2021-04-01 · 08:25–08:55)
1 The ostinato alone with a metronome, until you can talk over it 2 The other hand in the same rhythm on an easy scale; then triplets, sixteenths 3 A melody over it; then improvise 4 Under right-hand ostinato 3, change the harmony in the left: C, Cm, Dm, D7sus, D♭∆7♯11, G13sus, A♭ 5 Improvise the ostinato itself

Two-hand counterpoint drills

Build the left hand until the right hand can talk over it. (NK 2021-02-25 · 03:43–09:53; NK 2022-07-24 · 09:27–13:57)

"Countdown" (after Brad Mehldau) 1 Left hand 1 2 3 5 on every two-beat chord; 1 2 3 5 1 5 3 2 1 on a four-beat chord 2 Add the melody, then simple eighths on top 3 Alternate directions — up on one chord, down on the next 4 Hold each cell's first note through the chord; other cells: 1 3 5 1 Chord and scale 1 Right hand holds a voicing (Fm: 1 5 ♭3 11 ♭7 9); left hand runs F Dorian down and up, rubato; then through changes 2 Right hand moves its voicings in a rhythm while the left keeps running 3 A right-hand melody answered by left-hand lines; then lines in both hands — in 4ths, 3rds or arpeggios
Reference

Voicings, recipes, arpeggios.

The technical residue. Tap to expand each.

The exercise player — step it, hear it, move it

Every warmup on the page, playable. Step through one chord at a time, play the whole drill in tempo, or transpose it into any key — which is the only way these actually get learned.

Reds Spread & Quartal Voicings

+

Reds Spread. Step 1: four-note crunch in the left hand. Step 2: octave with perfect 5 in the right hand. The four-note crunch sets the harmonic frame; the octave-plus-5 gives it air. (OS clip Reds Spread · 00:00–00:23)

McCoy Tyner Quartals. Minor pentatonic in the right hand. Quartal voicings in the left (NK 2022-09-11 · 01:48–03:35):

  • In Dorian, the stacks on iii and vii contain a tritone; the rest are perfect fourths
  • Crunchy quartals — drop the bass tone by a half step (C–F–B♭ → C♭–F–B♭)
  • Crunchy quartals on the vi — drop both the bass tone and the first fourth (a-d-g → ab-db-g) (OS clip Crunchy Quartals · 01:42–07:49)

The same shape from the minor-pentatonic grip: Thin it to a quartal in NewJazz.

Kellman's pentatonic cycle. The minor pentatonic, transposed through itself — each note of the voicing moves to the next note of the scale (NK 2020-08-13 · 01:32–03:26):

1-4-♭7-♭3-5 → ♭3-5-1-4-♭7 → 4-♭7-♭3-5-1 → 5-1-4-♭7-♭3 → ♭7-♭3-5-1-4

First rotation in C minor pentatonic: C–F–B♭–E♭–G.

Also taught as Open Studio’s Magic Voicing System: the B♭ major pentatonic stacked a note apart is B♭6/9, and its five rotations also voice G–7, E♭∆7, C7sus and A♭∆7♯11. (OS workbook p.1–2; OS clip maness warmup pentatonic voicings · 00:00–00:44)

Also taught as three two-hand structures over C minor: the first rotation, C F B♭ E♭ G (“So What”), moved up a whole step; an F13 pivot, E♭ A D G C; then plain fourths, G C F B♭ E♭ → A D G C F. (OS clip osj three chord structures · 00:28–01:06)
