Nitai Hershkovits Studies

+

  1. Play up a scale with LH on the 7 and RH on the 3 — Alice Coltrane harp effect. In C: LH walks up scale starting on B, RH on E.

  2. Diatonic triads descending sequentially from the iii–. LH plays the 3 of the chord; RH plays 5, 3, 1, then descends. Shown over B♭– (B♭ minor): LH on D♭, RH octave B♭–F–B♭.

  3. Black-key bass diminished chords + white-key major/5: D♭/F · Cdim · B/D♯ · Bbdim · G/B · A7/E

    First chord — D♭/F (D♭ major triad over F bass).

  4. I∆ → V∆ via the IV (D to A via G). Diatonic triads in the right hand.

    Midpoint shown — G major triad with D bass connecting D∆ → A∆.

  5. D♭ → A♭ modulation chain: D♭6 → D♭°7 → D♭6 → F7 → B♭m → D♭m6/E → A♭/E♭ → E♭7 → A♭ → A♭7 → D♭6 → D♭°7 → C/D♭

    Pivot chord — D♭m6/E (D♭m6 with E in bass, a chromatic neighbor on the way to A♭).

  6. Pentatonic + chords: G minor pentatonic over A♭∆7 & E♭∆7, with color tones A♭, B, E.

  7. Over i (B♭m) play V7sus notes (F, A, B♭, C, E♭) with a light touch of D♭. Over iv (E♭m/G♭): E♭, F, G♭, A, B♭, with light touches of B and D♭.

    Over B♭m — F7sus notes in the RH (F A B♭ C E♭) with B♭m in the LH.

Arpeggios and their upper-structure formulas now have their own section: Arpeggios.

Thelonious Monk: surprise and the tritone

+

Two words for Monk's playing: surprise and the tritone. (NK 2022-10-30 · 02:44–17:59)

Tritone arpeggio 1 ♯4 over F7 (F B); on B♭7 fingers 3 1 3 1 Two-note clusters the 3 and ♯4 together under the thumb, mid-line "Melodic glitching" his name for it — jump an octave mid-line, drop in clusters and clashing intervals Whole tone fingers 1 2 3 · 1 2 3; a four-note pattern 1 2 3 4 moved up in whole steps Whole-tone approach enclosures from the whole-tone scale instead of chromatic ones — the chromatic version is Above, below, land in Blues Tritone-away arpeggio B7 over F7; a lick alternating F and B major triads Chords F7♯11 with the root on top and a natural 11 for the clash

Transcribed lines

+

Oscar Peterson, "Things Ain't What They Used to Be" (Night Train). The last phrase of a D♭ blues, Fm7 → B♭7 → E♭m7: E♭ A♭ C E♭ (♭7 ♭3 5 ♭7 of Fm7), then G♭, the ♭13 of B♭7, landing on the ♭3 of E♭m. Loop it slowed down and get the time feel before the speed. (NK 2022-11-20 · 09:04–12:28)

Ben Eunson on "Back Cycles". Over B∆ → Fm → E∆ → B♭7♯9♯5 → A∆ → E♭m → D∆ → A♭7♯9♯5: a B∆7 arpeggio, an Fm arpeggio, then the line leans into B♭alt before it arrives; over A♭, F and D major triads give the ♭9 and 13. With the chords this fast, treat some as passing and play as if there were half as many. (NK 2022-11-20 · 13:56–19:17)

Reharmonization Recipes

+

IV – vii – iii – vi – ii – V – I — the long cadence. The complete diatonic cycle of fourths. Every chord resolves down a fifth to the next.

Original IV — vii° — iii — vi — ii — V — I In C F∆7 — Bm7♭5 — Em7 — Am7 — Dm7 — G7 — C∆7

The Powell, tritone-sub, and five-step variants below operate on the iii–vi–ii–V–I tail of this cycle, but the full IV–vii preamble extends the same logic two chords earlier — and can be reharmed the same way.

The first move of the long cadence — F∆7 resolving down a fifth to Bm7♭5.

I → IV reharmonization, by stages. (OS clip I-IV reharmonizing · 00:00–00:51)

Stage 1 C∆7 → F∆7 Stage 2 + sec doms — Dm7 → G7 → C∆7 → Gm7 → C7 → F∆7 Stage 3 + 3rd in bass — A7/C♯ → Dm7 → G7 → C∆7 → D7/F♯ → Gm7 → C7 → F∆7 Stage 4 + ii before V/3-ii-V — Em7 → A7/C♯ → Dm7 → G7 → C∆7 → Am7 → D7/F♯ → Gm7 → C7 → F∆7 Stage 5 + tritone subs — Em7 → E♭7 → Dm7 → C♯7 → C∆7 → Am7 → A♭7 → Gm7 → F♯7 → F∆7

iii–vi–ii–V → Powell tritone subs. (OS clip budpowell substitution · 00:37–01:05)

Original iii — vi — ii — V — I All dominant III7alt — VI7alt — ii — V7 — I Powell iii — ♭III7 [tritone sub of vi] — ♭VI∆7 [tritone sub of ii] — ♭II∆7♯11 [tritone sub of V] — I Redux iii — ♭III7 — ♭VI∆7 — ♭II∆7♯11 — I

The chromatic descent it produces — Em7 → E♭7 → A♭∆7 → D♭∆7♯11 → C∆7, each root falling a half step or a fifth; only the substitute for vi stays a dominant.

iii–vi–ii–V–I with extended tritone subs. (OS note opstIG1; OS clip slip and slide tritone · 00:29–01:00)

B♭7(♯11) [tritone sub for iii] → A7(♯11♭9) [sec dom instead of vi → ii] → E♭7 [tritone sub for vi] → Dm7 → A♭7 → G7 → D♭7 → C∆ Redux ♭VII7♯11 — VI7♯11♭9 — ♭III7 — ii7 — ♭VI7 — V7 — ♭II7 — I∆

iii–vi–ii–V — five-step development. (OS clip reharmonizing · 00:00–00:56)

Step 1 Make all dominant Step 2 Tritone sub the iii Step 3 Tritone sub the vi Step 4 Descending ii–Vs Step 5 Sussed tritone subs e.g., Em7 → A7 → Dm7 → G7 ↓ E7(alt) → A7(alt) → D7(alt) → G7 ↓ B♭7♯11 → A7(alt) → D7(alt) → G7 ↓ E7 → E♭7/13 → D7 → G7 ↓ Em7 → A7 | E♭m7 → A♭7 | Dm7 → A♭7♯11 | G7 ↓ B♭13sus4 → A13sus4 → A♭13sus4 → G13sus4

Step 4 alone is also taught as a ii–V–I reharm (NK 2023-09-02 · 04:17–05:09). The final chromatic descent of sussed tritone subs:

NewJazz upper-structure shortcuts · ii7♭5♭9 — V7alt — im∆7.

Upper-structure triad pairs (♭VI & ♭VII over iiø7, ♭V & ♭VI over V7alt, IV & V over im6/9): see The triad pairs in NewJazz.

Six-note approach (the 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8 grip, twice per chord): see The right hand: 1 · 4 · 5 · 6 · 8, twice in NewJazz.

Backdoor. V7 → I replaced with ♭VII7 → I (G7 → B♭7 in C). Often spelled ♭VII7♯11 to call out the lydian dominant. Also taught with its ii — Fm7 → B♭7 → C∆7 — and a sus4 (E♭) resolving to the 3. (NK 2023-09-02 · 02:28–03:40)

7alt ↔ 13♯11 — see One grip, three roots in NewJazz.

Diminished System for Dominants

+

A °7 arpeggio is a rootless 7♭9 — for four dominants at once. Put a dominant root a half step below any of its notes: the same D♭ E G B♭ works over C7, E♭7, G♭7 and A7, supplying ♭9 3 5 ♭7 each time. So any 7♭9 can take a °7 arpeggio in the right hand — F7♭9 with C°7 (C E♭ G♭ A). Solo with the whole–half diminished scale a half step above the dominant's root: the same notes as the root's half–whole scale.

°7 arpeggio D♭ E G B♭ Root a ½ below C E♭ G♭ A Chord C7♭9 E♭7♭9 G♭7♭9 A7♭9

Also taught as a five-note voicing set: one E♭ “home” diminished shape in four inversions voices E♭°7, G♭°7, A°7 and C°7 — and F7♭9, A♭7♭9, B7♭9 and D7♭9. (OS workbook p.3–4)

F7♭9 in the left hand, the C°7 arpeggio sitting on top of it in the right. Worked example over one G bass: Diminished over ♭9 in The Barry Harris System.

In system C:

  • C°7 — a rootless voicing for four dominant chords
  • F°7 — the roots of those four dominants
  • G°7 — the roots of the four resolutions

The C°7 shape itself — C E♭ G♭ A. Symmetric, so all four inversions are the same shape moved a minor third.

The whole–half diminished scale a half step above the dominant's root — the scale to solo with:

An augmented triad works the same way, over three dominants. Put a dominant root on any of its notes: C E G♯ over C7, E7 and A♭7 supplies 1 3 ♯5 each time, and the accompaniment adds the ♭7 — a 7♯5 colour, which may rub against a natural 5th in the comping.

C7♯5 C E G♯ + B♭ E7♯5 E G♯ B♯ (= C) + D A♭7♯5 A♭ C E + G♭

Moving a whole pattern through these centers is sequencing: see 3 · 4 · 6 · 8 in practice in Playing Out.

Secondary dominant to diminished. (OS clip secondary dominants and secondary diminished · 00:03–00:14)

C∆7 → A7/C♯ [sec dom of ii] → B♭ [just the root, up ½] → Dm7 i.e., the ♭ii°7 emerges by just walking up a half step

The pivot moment — A7 with C♯ in the bass, one half step below the D of the Dm7 it lands on.

Substitutions & Passing Chords

+

Diatonic substitution. Chords that share enough tones to stand in for one another:

  • Rootless I∆7 (3, 5, 7, 9) = iii7 = V6
  • Rootless ii9 (♭3, 5, ♭7, 9) = IV∆7 = vi♭6
  • Rootless V13 (♭7, 9, 3, 13) = ii69 = rootless ♭II7♯9♭13
  • ii–V becomes Vsus7 — see Grip 1: move the bass a fifth in NewJazz
  • ii–V becomes IIIsus♭9

Rootless C∆9 — E G B D. The same four notes are an Em7, and a G6. Three names, one grip.

♭3-raised substitution — for all chords except the I:

ii–V–I becomes ii–V of ♭III e.g., for C: borrow the ii–V of E♭ (Fm7 as ii, B♭7 as V)

Diminished substitutions.

  • 7♭9 → the °7 a half step above, without the root (B♭7♭9 → B°7: B D F A♭ = ♭9 3 5 ♭7); over 7♯9 use the same diminished scale — see Diminished System for Dominants above
  • VI7alt can be ♯i°7
  • ∆+5 becomes dom7♭13

A♭°7 over a G bass — the rootless G7♭9. Drop the G and it's just the diminished shape.

Tritone substitution.

  • Any dom7 becomes the dom7 a tritone away — V7 becomes ♭II7, with its own ii: A♭m7 → D♭7 → C (NK 2023-09-02 · 03:40–04:17)
  • Any m7 or m7♭5 becomes a tritone dom7 — especially the ii of a ii–V–i
  • Also taught over the V's own bass — see Dissonance formulas in Playing Out
  • The VI or iv becomes a tritone dom7 — especially the vi of a vi–ii–V–i

D♭7 for G7 — the shared tritone is in red. B and F sit in both chords; only the root moves.

Secondary dominant. Each preceding chord becomes the V7 of the chord that follows:

iii–vi–ii–V–I → V7/vi – V7/ii – V7/V – V7 – I → III7 – VI7 – II7 – V7 – I

Unaltered dominants resolve to the major; altered dominants resolve to the minor. (OS clip mountain secondary dominants · 00:46–00:51)

Modal interchange.

  • Relative minor ⇄ relative major, and the rest of the borrowed family
  • I∆7 → ♭VII7
  • iii7 can become IIIsus♭9

By scale degree

On the I

  • Rootless I∆7 (3, 5, 7, 9) = iii7 = V6
  • Rootless ii9 (♭3, 5, ♭7, 9) = IV∆7 = vi♭6
  • I → iii–vi becomes I–IV–iii–vi before a ii–V–I
  • i6 in melodic minor becomes IV7♯11

On the ii

  • ii | V becomes ♯ii–♯V | ii–V (a chromatic ii–V approach)
  • ii–V becomes Vsus7
  • The ii of a ii–V becomes ii-∆7

On the V

  • The V of a ii–V becomes V7alt
  • ii–V becomes IIIsus♭9; V7 alone can also become IIIsus♭9
  • ii–V becomes IV7–♭VII7
  • ii–V becomes viiø7–III7
  • V–IV/V–iii (a descending bass line under the dominant)
  • Whole-tone chords function as V chords

On the VI7

  • VI7 becomes ♯i°
  • VI7 becomes ♭III7
  • A major chord ascending by whole tone becomes a major chord moving to the diminished a half-step above it (the same trick works descending)
